# illuminate

illuminate turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that illuminate applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate channel** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the user's
question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code, then
`illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Questions the user asks on the map
arrive later as illuminate channel messages; call `illuminate_next` for them. Don't edit files while working on a
request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open`
opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- As a Claude Code channel it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.


ARGUMENTS: how does the agent currently develop the visualisations based on a user's questions? dose it support hypothetical diagrams?

I've started making the map, and it should open in your browser in about a minute. If no tab appears, use this link: http://127.0.0.1:59206/m/agent-develop-visualisations-based-on-users?t=Qu0IKP15tvJOa4pYBPD8IDox

The illuminate channel didn't connect this session, so I ran `npm run illume` from this checkout. It uses the key in the checkout's `.env`. It stops by itself once you close the tab.

**How a map gets made, in short:**
1. **Head start:** a quick scan of the repo (`hints.ts`, using `@illuminate/facts`) lists every function by file, so Claude can cite names exactly as the checker knows them.
2. **Draft:** Claude explores the code with read-only tools and returns the map as structured JSON (`maker.ts`, prompts in `prompts.ts`, schema in `schemas.ts`).
3. **Check:** `check()` tests every box, arrow and "nothing does X" claim against the code.
4. **Repair:** claims that fail get up to two repair rounds, each sending only the changes. The best-checked version is kept.
5. **Follow-up questions** (`explainer.ts`) either answer from the map as it is, go back to the code (the only path that can add to the map or propose a fix), or offer a new map for a different part of the app. Additions that fail the check are dropped.

**Hypothetical diagrams: no, not as a feature.** By design, everything on a map has to match the code as it is now. There is no "what if" or "planned" kind of claim in `packages/core/src/format.ts`, and nothing in the prompts asks for one. The closest things are:
- **Missing arrows** (red dashed): a claim that something *isn't* connected, backed by a search the checker reruns.
- **Fixes:** Claude proposes a change, you approve it, and `applyFix` writes it. Only then does `connectAfterFix` draw the new arrow. As far as I can see, a proposed change isn't drawn on the map as a "would look like this" diagram before you approve it.

Adding hypotheticals would mean changing the map format, and CLAUDE.md treats that as the one change not to make casually, with tests. They'd also need a separate claim type the checker labels as not yet true, so the "everything shown matches the code" promise still holds. The map should confirm this from the code.

```text
**ship the backend version first**. The journey view is deferred, not dropped.
```

```text
1	# Handoff: where illuminate came from, what's decided, what's next
2	
3	Context for anyone (person or agent) picking illuminate up. The code and `README.md` say *what* exists; this says *why*,
4	what was learned along the way, and what's still open. As of 2026-11-02.
5	
6	## 1. The problem
7	
8	When you build mostly by directing AI agents, you lose your model of the system. Fixes become band-aids: each change is
9	judged locally ("did the error go away?") rather than against how the system is meant to work, and nobody notices the
10	same spot being patched five times. Call it **comprehension debt**: code that exists but that no person understands.
11	
12	The founding example is real. On an EHR workflow builder (care journeys, journey templates, automations such as "send
13	this email after the patient converts"), the concepts kept getting rewired, and the frontend looked finished. It was
14	impossible to tell how the backend was wired, or whether it was wired at all. *"I just trusted what I saw on the
15	frontend."*
16	
17	## 2. Who it's for
18	
19	- **Main user: semi-technical builders who ship with agents.** They know enough to act on what a map shows ("nothing
20	  listens for this event" is obviously a bug), but can't hold the whole system in their head. This group is growing
21	  fastest.
22	- **Not fully non-technical people.** They want "make it work and don't make me think about the backend", which works
23	  against the product. They're also mostly inside Lovable, Replit or Bolt, which own the screen.
24	- **Not senior engineers, mostly.** They already hold the model. The exception is an unfamiliar codebase.
25	- **Buyer later: teams and eng leads** worried about agent-written code nobody understands.
26	- **Framing:** it's not "leveling the playing field". It's "stay in control of what your agent builds, and get better
27	  at it as you go."
28	
29	## 3. What people said (Oct 2026 interviews)
30	
31	- **Jay** struggles with UX iteration; that's a different product, so leave it out. Separately, he worries whether V1 will
32	  hold up for V2 and V3, and has no visibility into the backend his technical cofounder owns. That suggests **the map as
33	  a shared language between a non-technical founder (who views and asks) and a technical cofounder (who acts).**
34	  Promise "you'll see where V2 will hurt", not "you'll know it scales".
35	- **The integration interviewee is the clearest signal.** He had to change a client's data integration, asked GPT how
36	  the workflow worked, and got a wall of text instead of a diagram. *Consultants working in client codebases* may be a
37	  sharp segment: they hit this on every new client.
38	- **The third person** plans heavily and says AI implements well "but…". The note cut off. **Follow up**: this is either
39	  the toughest customer or evidence that the pain is smaller for disciplined planners.
40	- **The bar to clear is "ask Claude for a Mermaid diagram".** That's free and solves maybe 60% of "wall of text". Illuminate
41	  has to win on things people notice: claims checked against the code, click-through to the code, the same drawing every
42	  time, and **showing what's missing**.
43	
44	## 4. What the user wants from the interface (direct feedback)
45	
46	- **Point at anything and ask.** Select a box, an arrow or a region; answers appear next to what was selected.
47	- **Plain English first.** Translating code into concepts *is* the value. Three depths: Concept, How it works, Code.
48	  Define jargon. Use a small concrete example from their own code.
49	  *(Later, Nov 2026: the three depths were dropped after trying them. Nobody opened the deeper two, and writing them
50	  made every answer slower. Replies are now a few plain sentences, the map does the explaining, and each box carries
51	  its code. The format still accepts `how` and `code` on boxes, so older maps load.)*
52	- **A real graph:** areas as containers, steps inside, labeled arrows between them. An early design with lane rows of
53	  blocks was rejected as "unintuitive, not an actual graph".
54	- **A walkthrough written with each map,** because a graph alone is hard to start reading. Stops go in the order that
55	  makes sense to a newcomer, and you can ask at every stop.
56	- **No "guess what happens next" prompts.** That idea was rejected.
57	- **The agent can fix things from the map**, not just explain them (see decision 5).
58	- **Model-agnostic is wanted.** The simplest version: illuminate runs its own Claude explainer, and any coding agent
59	  launches it.
60	- **Learning from walkthroughs:** a diagram of the user's own vibecoded architecture lost them. Every diagram needs its
61	  question and a line of context on top, 5 to 7 boxes at first with details on click, and plain labels.
62	
63	## 5. Design decisions and why
64	
65	1. **v1: Claude explores, a plain program checks.** No deterministic graph engine yet, because it isn't needed for
66	   "ask, get a map". Claude explores with Read/Grep/Glob and returns the map in a fixed format. `check()` re-reads every
67	   cited line and verifies calls, requests and imports against code facts. Later, the engine can replace the explorer
68	   behind the same format.
69	2. **The map format (`packages/core/src/format.ts`) is the one-way door.** Everything else is replaceable. Statuses are
70	   never stored; they're computed on every check.
71	3. **"Nothing does X" is a claim with proof.** Absences carry the search that proves them, and the checker reruns it.
72	   The missing connection is the bug people care about, and only a graph that can show absences can show it.
73	4. **Illuminate runs its own Claude explainer,** separate from the user's coding chat. It works with any agent and keeps
74	   explanation quality consistent. It can read the whole repo: the map is a starting point, not a fence. Anything it
75	   adds is drawn only if the checker confirms it.
76	   **Revised 2026-11-04 for the pilot: the Claude Code channel.** Products on the Agent SDK may not use people's
77	   claude.ai sign-in (Agent SDK overview and Legal and compliance pages), and pilot users shouldn't need an API key.
78	   So in Claude Code the user's own session is the explainer: `bridge.ts` is an `Agent` whose requests go to that
79	   session through the channel (`channel.ts`), and maker, explainer, fixes and `check()` are unchanged. The CLI with
80	   an API key stays for everything else (Codex, CI).
81	5. **Fixes:** Claude proposes. The fix is drawn as a green dashed arrow next to the exact diff. Nothing changes until
82	   approval. Then illuminate writes exactly that diff, refusing if the files changed since the proposal, re-checks the map,
83	   and offers Undo. Only one agent edits at a time. If illuminate is ever connected to the user's coding chat, that agent
84	   makes the edit instead.
85	6. **Delivery:** the basic version works everywhere through a skill, the `illume` CLI and a browser tab. Optional
86	   upgrades (not built):
87	   - **Channels:** Claude Code only, research preview. An MCP server pushes the user's question into the running chat.
88	   - **MCP Apps:** Cursor, VS Code Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop. The viewer embeds in the chat, and `ui/message` sends
89	     questions.
90	   - **Codex:** no documented way to push into a running session. Its desktop app has a Browser with an Annotate picker
91	     and WebMCP, which might allow something similar; untested.
92	7. **Local only:** binds to 127.0.0.1, a token is required, Host and Origin are checked, and secrets are never read.
93	
94	## 6. Graphify, for comparison (github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify, read at v0.9.97)
95	
96	- **Agent-facing.** Code goes to a graph through tree-sitter (no LLM). Query is keyword match, then BFS spreading in every
97	  direction. Clusters (Leiden) are named after their busiest node. Updates happen after commits, asynchronously, in
98	  seconds. There are no ordered flows, no fetch → route links, and no events or queues for JS. Its "benchmark" measures
99	  tokens, not task success. Graphify Cloud (YC S26) adds architecture rules.
100	- **Ideas worth borrowing:**
101	  - An edge counts as EXTRACTED only with import evidence; ambiguous matches are dropped rather than guessed.
102	  - Edges belong to the file they come from, so a change evicts only that file's edges.
103	  - Keep cluster IDs stable between rebuilds.
104	  - Stamp the graph with `built_at_commit`.
105	  - Hook messages phrased as facts, not commands. They found imperative wording gets ignored as prompt injection.
106	- **Don't build on it.** Illuminate's edge is everything it lacks.
107	
108	## 7. What's built (verified)
109	
110	- **Tests:** four packages, 102 tests, no model calls.
111	- **Viewer:** tested in Chrome with scripted Claude (`npm run preview`): making a map, the walkthrough, select and ask,
112	  a follow-up that adds checked steps, a fix (approve, reload, undo).
113	- **Real Claude, on the care-app fixture:**
114	  - The map came back 20 of 20 confirmed on the first pass, for about $0.21.
115	  - It also found a bug nobody planted: nothing ever starts the nightly job.
116	  - A real question cost about $0.14 and added two confirmed gaps.
117	  - A real fix cost about $0.24, was approved and applied, and re-checked 22 of 22.
118	- **Claude Code channel** (`illume channel`, 2026-11-04): tested with an MCP client in place of Claude Code
119	  (`test/channel.test.ts`: a map made in one turn, a question on the map pushed into the session and answered back) and
120	  over real stdio. **Not yet tried in a live Claude Code session.** A map request is about 3.5k tokens, even on
121	  scout-run.
122	- **Demo frontend:** `examples/care-app-ui/index.html`, the patient app as staff see it. Convert a patient and no welcome
123	  email arrives, even though the automation is active.
124	
125	## 8. Not built yet, and next steps
126	
127	- **Undo for an applied fix lasts only while the server runs.** Questions, answers and fix states are saved with the
128	  map (since 2026-11-03), and simple questions are answered from the map before Claude searches the code.
129	- **Hand-off to the user's coding agent:** the Claude Code channel is built (pilot users launch with
130	  `--dangerously-load-development-channels`); MCP Apps and a key-free mode for Codex are not.
131	- **Channel gaps:** the browser shows "Claude Code is working on this in your terminal" but not what Claude is reading;
132	  each new map opens a new tab; the read-only tools and the secret guard are only asked for, not enforced, since Claude
133	  uses its own session's tools. Ask Anthropic to put the channel on the allowlist before a wider launch.
134	- **Big repos are untested.** The head-start scan reads the whole repo.
135	- **Next, in order:**
136	  1. **Run Phase 0 with the integration interviewee:** his real question, illuminate vs "Claude + Mermaid" side by side.
137	  2. Try illuminate on a real repo, or a fresh Scout copy (`../scout-run`; never `../scout-agent`).
138	  3. Done 2026-11-03: off-topic questions offer a new map (or an answer in words), plus a map switcher. Next there: a
139	     routing test of 10–15 real questions with expected routes, run by hand since it uses Claude.
140	  4. Built 2026-11-04: the Claude Code channel. Next: try it live in Claude Code on care-app, then with pilot users.
141	  5. MCP Apps.
142	- **Later (Phase 3 of the plan):**
143	  - A fast graph engine with updates on every edit (incremental, LSP-style).
144	  - Live agent activity on the map.
145	  - "Working somewhere you haven't explored" and a per-user explored-regions map.
146	  - "This step was patched 5 times this week" counters. That's the *band-aid detector*, and it needs a time dimension.
147	
148	## 9. Gotchas that cost time
149	
150	- **Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` 0.3.296), verified from its types:**
151	  - The call is `query({ prompt, options: { cwd, model, tools, allowedTools, permissionMode: 'dontAsk', settingSources: [], strictMcpConfig, outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema }, resume, hooks } })`.
152	  - The answer arrives as `structured_output` on the `result` message.
153	  - PreToolUse hooks can return `permissionDecision` and `updatedInput`.
154	  - Auth is an API key or the Claude Code login.
155	- **React Flow 12:**
156	  - With controlled nodes, measurements live on `getInternalNode(id).measured`, not on your node objects.
157	  - Nodes that aren't selectable or draggable get `pointer-events: none` unless `onNodeClick` is set. Steps carry
158	    `nopan` so a pan doesn't swallow clicks.
159	- **ELK:** spacing options apply per container, so each area repeats them.
160	- **Chrome automation:**
161	  - A hidden tab renders no React Flow edges and drops input; check `document.visibilityState` and drive the page with
162	    in-page events.
163	  - The first click after a navigation is often dropped.
164	- **zsh `echo` mangles backslashes in JSON.** Write curl output to a file instead.
165	- **Channels with a custom server:**
166	  - Launch with `claude --dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>`. The flag is ignored under `-p` and the
167	    Agent SDK, so a channel can only be tried in an interactive session.
168	  - The server must log to stderr: stdout is the MCP connection (`runChannel` redirects `console.log`).
169	  - `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.2 negotiates at most protocol 2025-11-25, which stays clear of the 2026-07-28 problem below.
170	  - Claude Code won't register a channel server on MCP protocol 2026-07-28; `MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1` works around it.
171	  - The page needs its own sender check (a token): an ungated channel is a prompt-injection risk.
```

```text
1	// The map format: what Claude (or later the engine) writes, the checker verifies and the viewer draws.
2	// This is the one-way door. Statuses are never part of it: the checker computes them from the repo every time.
3	import { z } from 'zod';
4	
5	const Id = z.string().regex(/^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,64}$/, 'ids use letters, digits, _ . : - (at most 64)');
6	
7	/** A line of code that backs a claim. `text` must appear on that line (whitespace-insensitive) or within a few lines of it. */
8	export const Evidence = z.object({
9	  file: z.string().min(1),
10	  line: z.number().int().positive(),
11	  text: z.string().min(1).max(400),
12	});
13	
14	/** How a box is drawn: a way in (button, route, CLI), a step, a store (table, queue), something outside the repo, a job. */
15	export const NodeKind = z.enum(['entry', 'step', 'store', 'external', 'job']);
16	
17	/**
18	 * What an arrow claims. `calls`, `request` (fetch → route) and `imports` are also proven from code facts;
19	 * `then` (and anything the extractors can't see yet, like events) is proven by its evidence text alone.
20	 */
21	export const EdgeKind = z.enum(['calls', 'request', 'imports', 'then']);
22	
23	export const Area = z.object({ id: Id, label: z.string().min(1).max(40) });
24	
25	export const Node = z.object({
26	  id: Id,
27	  area: Id,
28	  kind: NodeKind.default('step'),
29	  name: z.string().min(1).max(80),
30	  /** `<file>#<symbol>` as the facts name it, e.g. `src/patients/service.ts#markConverted`. */
31	  symbol: z.string().regex(/^[^#]+#.+$/, 'symbol is <file>#<name>').optional(),
32	  explain: z.object({ concept: z.string(), how: z.string(), code: z.string() }).partial().optional(),
33	  evidence: z.array(Evidence).min(1),
34	});
35	
36	export const Edge = z.object({
37	  id: Id,
38	  from: Id,
39	  to: Id,
40	  kind: EdgeKind.default('then'),
41	  label: z.string().min(1).max(60),
42	  evidence: z.array(Evidence).min(1),
43	});
44	
45	/** A claim that something is missing, proven by a search the checker runs again: `matches` is the count claimed. */
46	export const Absence = z.object({
47	  id: Id,
48	  claim: z.string().min(1).max(200),
49	  /** Draw it as a missing arrow between these boxes. */
50	  between: z.object({ from: Id, to: Id }).optional(),
51	  search: z.object({
52	    pattern: z.string().min(1).max(200),
53	    regex: z.boolean().default(false),
54	    /** Globs to search; the whole repo when omitted. */
55	    paths: z.array(z.string().min(1)).optional(),
56	  }),
57	  matches: z.number().int().min(0),
58	});
59	
60	export const TourStop = z.object({
61	  id: Id,
62	  title: z.string().min(1).max(80),
63	  text: z.string().min(1).max(1200),
64	  focus: z.object({
65	    areas: z.array(Id).optional(),
66	    nodes: z.array(Id).optional(),
67	    edges: z.array(Id).optional(),
68	    absences: z.array(Id).optional(),
69	  }),
70	  terms: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
71	  ask: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
72	});
73	
74	export const CodeMap = z.object({
75	  version: z.literal(1),
76	  question: z.string().min(1).max(300),
77	  /** The commit the map was made from, when known. */
78	  commit: z.string().nullable().optional(),
79	  areas: z.array(Area).min(1),
80	  nodes: z.array(Node).min(1),
81	  edges: z.array(Edge).default([]),
82	  absences: z.array(Absence).default([]),
83	  tour: z.array(TourStop).default([]),
84	});
85	
86	export type Evidence = z.output<typeof Evidence>;
87	export type MapNode = z.output<typeof Node>;
88	export type MapEdge = z.output<typeof Edge>;
89	export type MapAbsence = z.output<typeof Absence>;
90	export type TourStop = z.output<typeof TourStop>;
91	export type CodeMap = z.output<typeof CodeMap>;
92	
93	export type ParseResult = { ok: true; map: CodeMap } | { ok: false; problems: string[] };
94	
95	/** A repo-relative path that can't climb out of the repo: no absolute paths, no `..`, no backslashes. */
96	export function isSafeRelativePath(path: string): boolean {
97	  if (!path || path.startsWith('/') || path.includes('\\') || /^[A-Za-z]:/.test(path)) return false;
98	  return path.split('/').every((seg) => seg !== '..' && seg !== '');
99	}
100	
101	/** Validates shape, then references: unique ids, edges between real boxes, tour stops that point at real things. */
102	export function parseMap(input: unknown): ParseResult {
103	  const parsed = CodeMap.safeParse(input);
104	  if (!parsed.success) {
105	    return { ok: false, problems: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join('.') || '(map)'}: ${i.message}`) };
106	  }
107	  const map = parsed.data;
108	  const problems: string[] = [];
109	  const ids = (kind: string, items: readonly { id: string }[]) => {
110	    const seen = new Set<string>();
111	    for (const { id } of items) {
112	      if (seen.has(id)) problems.push(`${kind} id "${id}" is used twice`);
113	      seen.add(id);
114	    }
115	    return seen;
116	  };
117	  const areas = ids('area', map.areas);
118	  const nodes = ids('node', map.nodes);
119	  const edges = ids('edge', map.edges);
120	  const absences = ids('absence', map.absences);
121	  ids('tour stop', map.tour);
122	
123	  const evidence = (where: string, list: readonly Evidence[]) => {
124	    for (const e of list) if (!isSafeRelativePath(e.file)) problems.push(`${where}: evidence file "${e.file}" must be a path inside the repo`);
125	  };
126	  for (const n of map.nodes) {
127	    if (!areas.has(n.area)) problems.push(`node "${n.id}": unknown area "${n.area}"`);
128	    if (n.symbol && !isSafeRelativePath(n.symbol.slice(0, n.symbol.indexOf('#')))) problems.push(`node "${n.id}": symbol file must be a path inside the repo`);
129	    evidence(`node "${n.id}"`, n.evidence);
130	  }
131	  for (const e of map.edges) {
132	    if (!nodes.has(e.from)) problems.push(`edge "${e.id}": unknown node "${e.from}"`);
133	    if (!nodes.has(e.to)) problems.push(`edge "${e.id}": unknown node "${e.to}"`);
134	    evidence(`edge "${e.id}"`, e.evidence);
135	  }
136	  for (const a of map.absences) {
137	    if (a.between && !nodes.has(a.between.from)) problems.push(`absence "${a.id}": unknown node "${a.between.from}"`);
138	    if (a.between && !nodes.has(a.between.to)) problems.push(`absence "${a.id}": unknown node "${a.between.to}"`);
139	  }
140	  for (const t of map.tour) {
141	    const refs: [string, readonly string[] | undefined, Set<string>][] = [
142	      ['area', t.focus.areas, areas], ['node', t.focus.nodes, nodes], ['edge', t.focus.edges, edges], ['absence', t.focus.absences, absences],
143	    ];
144	    for (const [kind, list, known] of refs) for (const id of list ?? []) if (!known.has(id)) problems.push(`tour stop "${t.id}": unknown ${kind} "${id}"`);
145	  }
146	  return problems.length ? { ok: false, problems } : { ok: true, map };
147	}
```

```text
// The one place illuminate talks to a model: a read-only Claude Agent SDK session that returns structured output.
// Read, Grep and Glob only; secret files are refused and left out of searches. Tests swap in a fake `Agent`.
import * as path from 'node:path';
import { query, type HookCallback, type PreToolUseHookInput } from '@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk';
import { isSecretPath } from '@illuminate/core';

export type Progress = { kind: 'read' | 'search' | 'list' | 'status'; text: string };

export type AgentRequest = {
  prompt: string;
  /** What this is for, in a few plain words ("Making the map for …"). Shown when the request is handed to Claude Code. */
  label?: string;
  schema: Record<string, unknown>;
  cwd: string;
  /** Continue an earlier session (follow-up questions keep what was already read). */
  resume?: string | null;
  model?: string;
  maxTurns?: number;
  /** Tools Claude may use: a subset of Read, Grep and Glob (default all three; `[]` for none, answering from the prompt). */
  tools?: readonly string[];
  onProgress?: (p: Progress) => void;
  signal?: AbortSignal;
};
export type AgentResponse = { output: unknown; sessionId: string | null; cost: number | null };
export type Agent = (req: AgentRequest) => Promise<AgentResponse>;

export const DEFAULT_MODEL = process.env.ILLUMINATE_MODEL ?? 'claude-opus-5-5';
const READ_ONLY = ['Read', 'Grep', 'Glob'];
/** ripgrep glob that leaves secret files out of a search the model didn't scope itself. */
const NOT_SECRETS = '!**/{.env,.env.*,*.pem,*.key,*.p12,id_rsa*,id_ed25519*,.npmrc,.netrc}';

/** A plain-English progress line for a tool call, with paths relative to the repo. */
export function progressOf(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>, cwd: string): Progress | null {
  const rel = (p: unknown) => (typeof p === 'string' ? path.relative(cwd, path.resolve(cwd, p)) || '.' : '');
  if (name === 'Read') return { kind: 'read', text: `Reading ${rel(input.file_path)}` };
  if (name === 'Grep') return { kind: 'search', text: `Searching for "${String(input.pattern ?? '')}"${input.path ? ` in ${rel(input.path)}` : ''}` };
  if (name === 'Glob') return { kind: 'list', text: `Looking for files matching ${String(input.pattern ?? '')}` };
  return null;
}

/** Refuse secret files, and keep repo-wide searches away from them. */
export function secretGuard(cwd: string): HookCallback {
  return async (input) => {
    const i = input as PreToolUseHookInput;
    const ti = (i.tool_input ?? {}) as Record<string, unknown>;
    const target = typeof ti.file_path === 'string' ? ti.file_path : typeof ti.path === 'string' ? ti.path : null;
    const rel = target ? path.relative(cwd, path.resolve(cwd, target)) : null;
    if (rel && (rel.startsWith('..') || path.isAbsolute(rel))) {
      return { hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: 'PreToolUse', permissionDecision: 'deny', permissionDecisionReason: 'Only files inside this repo can be read.' } };
    }
    if (rel && isSecretPath(rel)) {
      return { hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: 'PreToolUse', permissionDecision: 'deny', permissionDecisionReason: 'Secret files are never read.' } };
    }
    if (i.tool_name === 'Grep' && ti.glob === undefined && ti.type === undefined) {
      return { hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: 'PreToolUse', permissionDecision: 'allow', updatedInput: { ...ti, glob: NOT_SECRETS } } };
    }
    return {};
  };
}

export const sdkAgent: Agent = async (req) => {
  const abortController = new AbortController();
  req.signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => abortController.abort(), { once: true });
  // Never more than read-only, whatever the caller asks for.
  const tools = READ_ONLY.filter((t) => (req.tools ?? READ_ONLY).includes(t));
  const q = query({
    prompt: req.prompt,
    options: {
      cwd: req.cwd,
      model: req.model ?? DEFAULT_MODEL,
      tools,
      allowedTools: tools,
      permissionMode: 'dontAsk',
      settingSources: [],
      strictMcpConfig: true,
      outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema: req.schema },
      maxTurns: req.maxTurns ?? 60,
      abortController,
      hooks: { PreToolUse: [{ matcher: 'Read|Grep|Glob', hooks: [secretGuard(req.cwd)] }] },
      ...(req.resume ? { resume: req.resume } : {}),
```

```text
264	export async function runChannel(o: Omit<ChannelOptions, 'root'> & { root?: string }) {
265	  console.log = console.error;
266	  console.info = console.error;
267	  const channel = createChannel({ ...o, root: o.root ?? process.env.CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR ?? process.cwd() });
268	  let stopping = false;
269	  const stop = () => {
270	    if (stopping) return;
271	    stopping = true;
272	    void channel.close().finally(() => process.exit(0));
273	  };
274	  channel.mcp.onclose = stop;
275	  process.on('SIGINT', stop);
276	  process.on('SIGTERM', stop);
277	  await channel.mcp.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
```

```text
1	// An `Agent` that is the person's own Claude Code session, reached through a channel. Each call becomes a request that
2	// waits until Claude Code submits output for it (or gives up). The maker, explainer and checker don't know the
3	// difference: they get output back exactly as from `sdkAgent`, and everything still goes through `check()`.
4	//
5	// A request reaches Claude Code one of two ways: handed to a tool call that is waiting for the next piece of work (so
6	// Claude carries straight on within one turn), or, when none is waiting, announced so the channel can push a message
7	// into the session.
8	import type { Agent, AgentRequest, AgentResponse } from './agent';
9	import { validatorFor } from './schemas';
10	
11	export type BridgeRequest = {
12	  id: string;
13	  label: string;
14	  prompt: string;
15	  schema: Record<string, unknown>;
16	  /** Tools the request may use; `[]` means answer from the request alone, without reading the code. */
17	  tools: readonly string[];
18	  /** It follows on from earlier work in the same conversation (a repair round, a follow-up question). */
19	  continues: boolean;
20	};
21	
22	type Entry = BridgeRequest & { handed: boolean; resolve: (r: AgentResponse) => void; reject: (e: Error) => void };
23	export type SubmitResult = { ok: true } | { ok: false; problems: string[] };
24	
25	export type Bridge = {
26	  agent: Agent;
27	  /** The oldest request Claude hasn't been handed yet, or else the oldest still waiting for output. Marks it handed. */
28	  next(): BridgeRequest | null;
29	  /** The next request to hand over: now if one is waiting, else the next one made, or null when `signal` aborts. */
30	  waitForNext(signal: AbortSignal): Promise<BridgeRequest | null>;
31	  submit(id: string, output: unknown): SubmitResult;
32	  fail(id: string, reason: string): boolean;
33	  /** Requests still waiting for output. */
34	  outstanding(): BridgeRequest[];
35	};
36	
37	export const CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION = 'claude-code';
38	
39	const view = (e: Entry): BridgeRequest => ({ id: e.id, label: e.label, prompt: e.prompt, schema: e.schema, tools: e.tools, continues: e.continues });
40	
41	export function createBridge(o: { announce: (r: BridgeRequest) => void }): Bridge {
42	  const entries: Entry[] = [];
43	  const waiters: ((r: Entry) => void)[] = [];
44	  let n = 0;
45	
46	  const agent: Agent = (req: AgentRequest) =>
47	    new Promise<AgentResponse>((resolve, reject) => {
48	      if (req.signal?.aborted) return reject(new Error('Stopped.'));
49	      const entry: Entry = {
50	        id: `r${++n}`,
51	        label: req.label ?? 'Work for illuminate',
52	        prompt: req.prompt,
53	        schema: req.schema,
54	        tools: req.tools ?? ['Read', 'Grep', 'Glob'],
55	        continues: !!req.resume,
56	        handed: false,
57	        resolve,
58	        reject,
59	      };
60	      entries.push(entry);
61	      req.signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => {
62	        const i = entries.indexOf(entry);
63	        if (i >= 0) entries.splice(i, 1);
64	        reject(new Error('Stopped.'));
65	      }, { once: true });
66	      req.onProgress?.({ kind: 'status', text: 'Claude Code is working on this in your terminal' });
67	      const waiter = waiters.shift();
68	      if (waiter) {
69	        entry.handed = true;
70	        waiter(entry);
71	      } else {
72	        o.announce(view(entry));
73	      }
74	    });
75	
76	  const take = (): Entry | null => {
77	    const e = entries.find((x) => !x.handed) ?? null;
78	    if (e) e.handed = true;
79	    return e;
80	  };
81	
82	  return {
83	    agent,
84	    next() {
85	      const e = take() ?? entries[0] ?? null;
86	      return e ? view(e) : null;
87	    },
88	    waitForNext(signal) {
89	      const now = take();
90	      if (now) return Promise.resolve(view(now));
91	      if (signal.aborted) return Promise.resolve(null);
92	      return new Promise((resolve) => {
93	        const waiter = (e: Entry) => {
94	          signal.removeEventListener('abort', onAbort);
95	          resolve(view(e));
96	        };
97	        const onAbort = () => {
98	          const i = waiters.indexOf(waiter);
99	          if (i >= 0) waiters.splice(i, 1);
100	          resolve(null);
101	        };
102	        waiters.push(waiter);
103	        signal.addEventListener('abort', onAbort, { once: true });
104	      });
105	    },
106	    submit(id, output) {
107	      const e = entries.find((x) => x.id === id);
108	      if (!e) return { ok: false, problems: [`No request "${id}" is waiting. It may have been answered already, or stopped.`] };
109	      let value = output;
110	      if (typeof value === 'string') {
111	        try {
112	          value = JSON.parse(value);
113	        } catch {
114	          return { ok: false, problems: ['`output` must be a JSON object matching the schema, not text.'] };
115	        }
116	      }
117	      const validator = validatorFor(e.schema);
118	      if (validator) {
119	        const parsed = validator.safeParse(value);
120	        if (!parsed.success) {
121	          return { ok: false, problems: parsed.error.issues.slice(0, 12).map((i) => `${i.path.join('.') || '(output)'}: ${i.message}`) };
122	        }
123	      } else if (!value || typeof value !== 'object' || Array.isArray(value)) {
124	        return { ok: false, problems: ['`output` must be a JSON object matching the schema.'] };
125	      }
126	      entries.splice(entries.indexOf(e), 1);
127	      // The raw value, not zod's output: callers parse it themselves, exactly as they do structured output.
128	      e.resolve({ output: value, sessionId: CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION, cost: null });
129	      return { ok: true };
130	    },
131	    fail(id, reason) {
132	      const e = entries.find((x) => x.id === id);
133	      if (!e) return false;
134	      entries.splice(entries.indexOf(e), 1);
135	      e.reject(new Error(`Claude Code couldn't finish this: ${reason}`));
136	      return true;
137	    },
138	    outstanding: () => entries.map(view),
139	  };
140	}
```

<fetched-web-content>
> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Push events into a running session with channels

> Use channels to push messages, alerts, and webhooks into your Claude Code session from an MCP server. Forward CI results, chat messages, and monitoring events so Claude can react while you're away.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Channels are in [research preview](#research-preview). They require Anthropic authentication through claude.ai or a Console API key, and are not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. Team and Enterprise organizations must [explicitly enable them](#enterprise-controls).

A channel is an MCP server that pushes events into your running Claude Code session, so Claude can react to things that happen while you're not at the terminal. Channels can be two-way: Claude reads the event and replies back through the same channel, like a chat bridge. Events only arrive while the session is open, so for an always-on setup you run Claude in a background process or persistent terminal.

Unlike integrations that spawn a fresh cloud session or wait to be polled, the event arrives in the session you already have open: see [how channels compare](#how-channels-compare).

You install a channel as a plugin and configure it with your own credentials. Telegram, Discord, and iMessage are included in the research preview.

When Claude replies through a channel, you see the inbound message in your terminal but not the reply text. The terminal shows the tool call and a confirmation (like "sent"), and the actual reply appears on the other platform.

If you manage a Team, Enterprise, or Console organization, see [Enable channels for your organization](#enterprise-controls). To build your own channel, see the [Channels reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md).

## Supported channels

Each supported channel is a plugin that requires [Bun](https://bun.sh). For a hands-on demo of the plugin flow before connecting a real platform, try the [fakechat quickstart](#quickstart).

> [tab] Telegram
>

## Quickstart

Fakechat is an officially supported demo channel that runs a chat UI on localhost, with nothing to authenticate and no external service to configure.

Once you install and enable fakechat, you can type in the browser and the message arrives in your Claude Code session. Claude replies, and the reply shows up back in the browser. After you've tested the fakechat interface, try out [Telegram](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/telegram), [Discord](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/discord), or [iMessage](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/imessage).

To try the fakechat demo, you'll need:

* Claude Code [installed and authenticated](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart.md#step-1-install-claude-code) with a claude.ai account or a Claude Console API key
* [Bun](https://bun.sh) installed. The pre-built channel plugins are Bun scripts. Check with `bun --version`; if that fails, [install Bun](https://bun.sh/docs/installation).
* **Team, Enterprise, or managed Console org**: your admin must [enable channels](#enterprise-controls) in managed settings

**1. Install the fakechat channel plugin**

Start Claude Code by running `claude` in your terminal, then enter the install command at its prompt:

```text theme={null}
/plugin install fakechat@claude-plugins-official
```

If the install fails, match the message Claude Code reports:

* `Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found`: add the marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install.
* `Plugin "<name>" not found in marketplace "claude-plugins-official"`: your local copy of the marketplace catalog may be out of date. Refresh it with `/plugin marketplace update claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install. If the retry prints the same message, see [Plugin not found in marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#plugin-not-found-in-marketplace).

When the install asks for an installation scope, choose the user scope option so the plugin is available across all your projects.

If the install summary reports `Run /reload-plugins to apply.`, you don't need to act on it here, because restarting in the next step picks up the plugin.

**2. Restart with the channel enabled**

Exit Claude Code, then restart with `--channels` and pass the fakechat plugin you installed:

```bash theme={null}
claude --channels plugin:fakechat@claude-plugins-official
```

The fakechat server starts automatically. The startup screen shows a channels notice stating that messages from `plugin:fakechat@claude-plugins-official` inject directly in this session. If the plugin isn't installed or isn't on the approved allowlist, a warning line naming the problem appears below that notice.

> [!TIP]
>
> You can pass several plugins to `--channels`, space-separated.

**3. Push a message in**

Open the fakechat UI at [http://localhost:8787](http://localhost:8787) and type a message:

```text theme={null}
what's in my working directory?
```

The message arrives in your Claude Code session. The terminal shows it as an inbound channel line like `← fakechat · web: what's in my working directory?`, while the model receives it as a `<channel source="plugin:fakechat:fakechat">` event, using the plugin's scoped server name. Claude reads it, does the work, and calls fakechat's `reply` tool. If Claude Code asks for permission for the first reply, approve it. The answer shows up in the chat UI.

If Claude hits a permission prompt while you're away from the terminal, the session pauses until you respond. Channel servers that declare the [permission relay capability](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#relay-permission-prompts) can forward these prompts to you so you can approve or deny remotely. For unattended use, [`--dangerously-skip-permissions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) bypasses most prompts, but only use it in environments you trust. Even then, the [actions no mode auto-approves](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#actions-no-mode-auto-approves) still apply.

When you run channels in non-interactive mode with `-p`, tools that need terminal input, such as multiple-choice questions and plan mode approval, are disabled so the session never stalls waiting for input.

## Security

Every approved channel plugin maintains a sender allowlist: only IDs you've added can push messages, and everyone else is silently dropped.

Telegram and Discord bootstrap the list by pairing:

1. Find your bot in Telegram or Discord and send it any message
2. The bot replies with a pairing code
3. In your Claude Code session, approve the code when prompted
4. Your sender ID is added to the allowlist

iMessage works differently: texting yourself bypasses the gate automatically, and you add other contacts by handle with `/imessage:access allow`.

On top of that, you control which servers are enabled each session with `--channels`, and your organization controls availability with [`channelsEnabled`](#enterprise-controls) on claude.ai Team and Enterprise plans and on Console organizations that deploy managed settings.

Being in `.mcp.json` isn't enough to push messages: a server also has to be named in `--channels`.

The allowlist also gates [permission relay](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#relay-permission-prompts) if the channel declares it. Anyone who can reply through the channel can approve or deny tool use in your session, so only allowlist senders you trust with that authority.

## Enterprise controls

Admins control availability through two [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md) that users cannot override. The default depends on how you authenticate:

* **claude.ai Team and Enterprise**: channels are blocked until an Owner [enables them](#enable-channels-for-your-organization).
* **Anthropic Console with API key authentication**: channels are permitted by default. You only need this setting if your organization deploys managed settings.

In all cases, no channel runs until a user opts it in for the session with `--channels`.

| Setting | Purpose | When not configured |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `channelsEnabled` | Master switch. Must be `true` for any channel to deliver messages. Blocks all channels including the development flag when off. See [Enable channels for your organization](#enable-channels-for-your-organization). | claude.ai Team and Enterprise: channels blocked. Console: channels allowed unless your organization deploys managed settings, in which case channels are blocked until this key is set |
| `allowedChannelPlugins` | Which plugins can register once channels are enabled. Replaces the Anthropic-maintained list when set. | Anthropic default list applies |

Pro, Max, and Ultra users without an organization skip these checks entirely: channels are available and users opt in per session with `--channels`.

### Enable channels for your organization

Enable channels for your organization from [**Organization settings > Claude Code > Channels**](https://claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code), which requires the Owner role, or by setting `channelsEnabled` to `true` in managed settings.

Once enabled, users in your organization can use `--channels` to opt channel servers into individual sessions. If the setting is disabled or unset, the MCP server still connects and its tools work, but channel messages won't arrive. A startup warning tells the user to have an admin enable the setting.

### Restrict which channel plugins can run

By default, any plugin on the Anthropic-maintained allowlist can register as a channel. Admins on Team and Enterprise plans can replace that allowlist with their own by setting `allowedChannelPlugins` in managed settings. Use this to restrict which official plugins are allowed, approve channels from your own internal marketplace, or both. Each entry names a plugin and the marketplace it comes from:

```json theme={null}
{
  "channelsEnabled": true,
  "allowedChannelPlugins": [
    { "marketplace": "claude-plugins-official", "plugin": "telegram" },
    { "marketplace": "claude-plugins-official", "plugin": "discord" },
    { "marketplace": "acme-corp-plugins", "plugin": "internal-alerts" }
  ]
}
```

If you set an empty array, you block all channel plugins from the allowlist, but `--dangerously-load-development-channels` can still bypass that block for local testing. To block channels entirely including the development flag, leave `channelsEnabled` unset instead.

This setting requires `channelsEnabled: true`. If a user passes a plugin to `--channels` that isn't on your list, Claude Code starts normally but the channel doesn't register, and the startup notice explains that the plugin isn't on the organization's approved list. On the v2 MCP client runtime, a channel can also fail to register because Claude Code [doesn't register a channel server that negotiates protocol revision 2026-07-28](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#push-messages-with-channels).

## Research preview

Channels are a research preview feature. Availability is rolling out gradually, and the `--channels` flag syntax and protocol contract may change based on feedback.

Neither `--channels` nor `--dangerously-load-development-channels` appears in `claude --help` while the feature is in preview. The flags work even though they aren't listed.

During the preview, `--channels` only accepts plugins from an Anthropic-maintained allowlist, or from your organization's allowlist if an admin has set [`allowedChannelPlugins`](#restrict-which-channel-plugins-can-run). The channel plugins in [claude-plugins-official](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins) are the default approved set. If you pass something that isn't on the effective allowlist, Claude Code starts normally but the channel doesn't register, and the startup notice tells you why.

To test a channel you're building, pass it to `--dangerously-load-development-channels` in the `plugin:<name>@<marketplace>` or `server:<name>` form. See [Test during the research preview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#test-during-the-research-preview) for information about testing custom channels that you build.

Report issues or feedback on the [Claude Code GitHub repository](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues).

## How channels compare

Several Claude Code features connect to systems outside the terminal, each suited to a different kind of work:

| Feature | What it does | Good for |
| - | - | - |
| [Cloud sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md) | Run tasks in a fresh cloud sandbox, cloned from GitHub | Delegating self-contained async work you check on later |
| [Claude in Slack](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slack.md) | Spawns a cloud session from an `@Claude` mention in a channel or thread | Starting tasks directly from a team conversation |
| Standard [MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md) | Claude queries it during a task; nothing is pushed to the session | Giving Claude on-demand access to read or query a system |
| [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md) | You drive your local session from claude.ai or the Claude mobile app | Steering an in-progress session while away from your desk |

Channels fill the gap in that list by pushing events from non-Claude sources into your already-running local session.

* **Chat bridge**: ask Claude something from your phone via Telegram, Discord, or iMessage, and the answer comes back in the same chat while the work runs on your machine against your real files.
* **[Webhook receiver](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#example-build-a-webhook-receiver)**: a webhook from CI, your error tracker, a deploy pipeline, or other external service arrives where Claude already has your files open and remembers what you were debugging.

## Next steps

Once you have a channel running, explore these related features:

* [Build your own channel](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md) for systems that don't have plugins yet
* [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md) to drive a local session from your phone instead of forwarding events into it
* [Session-scoped scheduled tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks.md) to poll on a timer instead of reacting to pushed events
