# Environment variables

> Reference for environment variables that control Claude Code behavior.

Environment variables can control Claude Code behavior such as model selection, authentication, request routing, and feature toggles. Many of the same behaviors can also be configured through a [settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md) field, a [CLI flag](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.md), or an in-session command like `/model`.

This page covers how to:

* [Set environment variables](#set-environment-variables) in your shell or in a settings file
* [Check which value applies](#precedence) when a behavior can be set more than one way
* [Look up the variables Claude Code reads](#variables)
* [See which features stop working](#features-that-need-feature-flag-fetching) when a variable turns feature-flag fetching off

## Set environment variables

A variable you set in your shell lasts for that terminal session, while a variable in a settings file applies every time `claude` runs.

### Set variables in your shell

Set the variable before launching `claude`:

> [tab] macOS, Linux, WSL
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> export API_TIMEOUT_MS="1200000"
> claude
> ```
>
> To set it for every session, add the `export` line to `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, or your shell's profile file.

> [tab] Windows PowerShell
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> $env:API_TIMEOUT_MS = "1200000"
> claude
> ```
>
> To set it for every session, run `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("API_TIMEOUT_MS", "1200000", "User")` and open a new terminal.

> [tab] Windows CMD
>
> ```batch theme={null}
> set API_TIMEOUT_MS=1200000
> claude
> ```
>
> To set it for every session, run `setx API_TIMEOUT_MS "1200000"` and open a new terminal.

The assignment line prints nothing on success. To confirm the variable is set, print it in the same shell:

> [tab] macOS, Linux, WSL
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> echo $API_TIMEOUT_MS
> ```

> [tab] Windows PowerShell
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> echo $env:API_TIMEOUT_MS
> ```

> [tab] Windows CMD
>
> ```batch theme={null}
> echo %API_TIMEOUT_MS%
> ```

### Set variables in settings files

Add variables under the `env` key in a `settings.json` file, creating the file if it doesn't exist. Claude Code reads them directly from the file, so they take effect no matter how `claude` was launched. A running session applies new and changed values to its environment when you save the file, but a feature that reads its variables once at startup, such as [OpenTelemetry monitoring](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage.md), keeps its startup values until you relaunch. Removing a variable from the file doesn't unset it in a running session; the removal takes effect the next time you launch `claude`.

```json ~/.claude/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "env": {
    "API_TIMEOUT_MS": "1200000",
    "BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS": "300000"
  }
}
```

Claude Code copies these values into its environment as written. No shell processes them, so shorthand such as `~` or `$HOME` stays as typed. For a variable that takes a path, such as `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, write the absolute path: `"CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR": "/home/you/.claude-work"`.

The file you choose controls who the variables apply to:

| File | Applies to |
| :- | :- |
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | You, in every project |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Everyone working in the project, checked into source control |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` | You, in this project only, gitignored when Claude Code saves a setting to it; add it to your gitignore if you create it by hand |
| Managed settings | Everyone in your organization, deployed by an admin |

See [Settings files](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#where-settings-live) for where each file lives and [Settings precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#settings-precedence) for how they combine when more than one sets the same variable.

## Precedence

Some behaviors have both an environment variable and a dedicated settings key, and which one Claude Code reads first differs per key. For `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` and `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_CONNECT_IDE`, Claude Code reads the variable first and uses the `model` or `autoConnectIde` setting only when the variable is unset. For the pair you're setting, check the variable's row below and the key's entry on the [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md).

When the same variable is set in both your shell and a settings file `env` block, the settings file value applies in most sessions. Claude Code writes each `env` entry into the process environment, replacing the value inherited from the shell. [How `env` values interact with your shell](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#how-env-values-interact-with-your-shell) covers the sessions that keep the inherited value instead, and the [`env` setting](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#when-claude-code-applies-env-values) says when it applies them. A few variables are special-cased; the [`env` setting](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#env) lists the exceptions.

In a settings file you can set a variable but you can't remove one. To override a variable you can't unset, such as a stale `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` exported by a shell profile you don't control, set it to an empty string in the `env` block: `"CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX": ""`. Claude Code treats the empty value as unset for provider selection. Subprocesses still inherit the empty value.

Between settings files, `env` values follow [settings precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#settings-precedence), so a managed settings entry overrides the same variable in user or project settings. Project and local settings can't set some variables, such as `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and the OpenTelemetry exporter variables. [Variables Claude Code ignores in `env`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env) lists them, along with the OpenTelemetry off values that still apply.

How an environment variable interacts with CLI flags and in-session commands varies per feature: `--model` and `/model` override `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, while `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` overrides `--effort` and `/effort`. When a variable interacts with another configuration source, its row in the [Variables](#variables) list states the precedence or links to the page that documents it.

Claude Code reads shell environment variables at startup, so changes to them take effect the next time you launch `claude`. Variables set under the `env` key in settings files are reapplied to a running session when the file changes, with the startup-only exception described in [Set variables in settings files](#in-settings-files).

## Variables

Numeric variables such as timeouts, token budgets, and retry counts accept scientific notation and digit-separator spellings in addition to plain digits, except where a variable's row notes it takes plain digits only. For example, Claude Code reads `2e3` as 2000 and `64_000` as 64000. Before v2.1.211, these spellings could silently set a much smaller value, such as `1e6` setting a timeout to 1.

> [!NOTE]
>
> For variables that turn a behavior on or off, set `1`, `true`, `yes`, or `on` to turn it on and `0`, `false`, `no`, or `off` to turn it off, in any casing.
>
> Some variables read only whether you set them at all, so any non-empty value including `0` turns the behavior on, and you turn the behavior off by unsetting the variable or setting it to an empty value. These variables work that way:
>
> * `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC`
> * `DISABLE_TELEMETRY`
> * `DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING`
> * `CLAUDE_CODE_TMUX_TRUECOLOR`
> * `IS_DEMO`
>
> Each variable's row also states its own rule.

| Variable | Purpose |
| :- | :- |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | API key sent as `X-Api-Key` header. When set, this key is used instead of your Claude Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise subscription even if you are logged in. In non-interactive mode (`-p`), the key is always used when present. In interactive mode, you are prompted to approve the key once before it overrides your subscription. To use your subscription instead, run `unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | Custom value for the `Authorization` header (the value you set here will be prefixed with `Bearer `) |
| `ANTHROPIC_AWS_API_KEY` | Workspace API key for [Claude Platform on AWS](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-platform-on-aws.md), generated in the AWS Console. Sent as `x-api-key` and takes precedence over AWS SigV4 |
| `ANTHROPIC_AWS_BASE_URL` | Override the [Claude Platform on AWS](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-platform-on-aws.md) endpoint URL. Use for custom regions or when routing through an [LLM gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway). Defaults to `https://aws-external-anthropic.{region}.api.aws`. Claude Code resolves the region with the [same precedence as on Amazon Bedrock](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md#3-configure-claude-code) |
| `ANTHROPIC_AWS_WORKSPACE_ID` | Required for [Claude Platform on AWS](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-platform-on-aws.md). Sent on every request as the `anthropic-workspace-id` header |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | Override the API endpoint to route requests through a proxy or gateway. For what happens when that gateway rejects MCP tool search, see [Tool search through an LLM gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#tool-search-through-a-gateway). As of v2.1.196, [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md#requirements) is disabled when this points at a host other than `api.anthropic.com`, matching its behavior on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry |
| `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL` | Override the Amazon Bedrock endpoint URL. Use for custom Amazon Bedrock endpoints or when routing through an [LLM gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway). See [Amazon Bedrock](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md) |
| `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_MANTLE_BASE_URL` | Override the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint URL. See [Mantle endpoint](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md#use-the-mantle-endpoint) |
| `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX` | Cross-region inference profile prefix (`us`, `eu`, `apac`, `jp`, `au`, or `global`) Claude Code tries first instead of the one derived from the AWS region. Ignored in AWS GovCloud regions. Requires Claude Code v2.1.224 or later. See [Amazon Bedrock](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md#cross-region-inference-profile-prefixes) |
| `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_SERVICE_TIER` | Amazon Bedrock [service tier](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html) (`default`, `flex`, or `priority`). See [Amazon Bedrock](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md#service-tiers) |
| `ANTHROPIC_BETAS` | Comma-separated list of additional `anthropic-beta` header values to include in API requests. Claude Code already sends the beta headers it needs; use this to opt into an [Anthropic API beta](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/beta-headers) before Claude Code adds native support. Unlike the [`--betas` flag](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags), which requires API key authentication, this variable works with all auth methods including Claude.ai subscription |
| `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS` | Custom headers to add to requests (`Name: Value` format, newline-separated for multiple headers). If a name or value contains a character an HTTP header can't carry, such as a curly quote or a zero-width space, the request fails with an error that identifies the pair by position. Requires Claude Code v2.1.227 or later. [Invalid request header value](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#invalid-request-header-value) lists the exact character set and where the check runs. A value that sets a credential, org or tenant, routing, or API-behavior header, such as `Authorization` or `Host`, counts as a [setting that needs approval](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/server-managed-settings.md#environment-variables-and-the-approval-dialog) when server-managed settings deliver it. From project or local settings, such a value follows the [rules for when `env` values apply](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#when-claude-code-applies-env-values) |
| `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION` | Model ID to add as a custom entry in the `/model` picker. Use this to make a non-standard or gateway-specific model selectable without replacing built-in aliases. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#add-a-custom-model-option) |
| `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_DESCRIPTION` | Display description for the custom model entry in the `/model` picker. Defaults to `Custom model (<model-id>)` when not set |
| `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_NAME` | Display name for the custom model entry in the `/model` picker. When not set, the entry shows the model's name if Claude Code [recognizes the ID](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities), and the model ID otherwise |
| `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` | Comma-separated list of [capabilities](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) the custom model supports, for example `effort,thinking`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL` | Model ID that the `fable` alias resolves to, and the ID Claude Code recognizes as a Fable model for [automatic model fallback](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#automatic-model-fallback) on third-party providers. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#environment-variables) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL_DESCRIPTION` | Display description for the pinned Fable model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows a default description that begins `Custom Fable model`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL_NAME` | Display name for the pinned Fable model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows the model's name if Claude Code recognizes the pinned ID, and the pinned ID otherwise. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` | Comma-separated list of [capabilities](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) the pinned Fable model supports, for example `effort,thinking`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` | Model ID that the `haiku` alias resolves to, also used for [background functionality](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs.md#background-token-usage). See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#environment-variables) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL_DESCRIPTION` | Display description for the pinned Haiku model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows a default description that begins `Custom Haiku model`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL_NAME` | Display name for the pinned Haiku model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows the model's name if Claude Code recognizes the pinned ID, and the pinned ID otherwise. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` | Comma-separated list of [capabilities](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) the pinned Haiku model supports, for example `effort,thinking`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` | Model that new sessions start on by default. Requires Claude Code v2.1.236 or later. See [Set a default model for new sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#set-a-default-model-for-new-sessions) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL` | Model ID that the `opus` alias resolves to, and that `opusplan` uses while Plan Mode is active. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#environment-variables) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_DESCRIPTION` | Display description for the pinned Opus model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows a default description that begins `Custom Opus model`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_NAME` | Display name for the pinned Opus model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows the model's name if Claude Code recognizes the pinned ID, and the pinned ID otherwise. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` | Comma-separated list of [capabilities](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) the pinned Opus model supports, for example `effort,thinking`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL` | Model ID that the `sonnet` alias resolves to, and that `opusplan` uses when Plan Mode is not active. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#environment-variables) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_DESCRIPTION` | Display description for the pinned Sonnet model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows a default description that begins `Custom Sonnet model`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_NAME` | Display name for the pinned Sonnet model in the `/model` picker. When not set, the row shows the model's name if Claude Code recognizes the pinned ID, and the pinned ID otherwise. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_SUPPORTED_CAPABILITIES` | Comma-separated list of [capabilities](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) the pinned Sonnet model supports, for example `effort,thinking`. See [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#customize-pinned-model-display-and-capabilities) |
| `ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID` | Federation rule ID for [Workload Identity Federation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation). When you set it together with `ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID`, Claude Code selects federation credentials, which rank above your `/login` credential. See [authentication precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.md#authentication-precedence) |
| `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_API_KEY` | API key for Microsoft Foundry authentication (see [Microsoft Foundry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/microsoft-foundry.md)) |
| `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_AUTH_TOKEN` | Bearer token for Microsoft Foundry authentication, such as a Microsoft Entra access token. Claude Code sends it as the `Authorization: Bearer` header. Takes precedence over `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_API_KEY` and over the Azure default credential chain. See [Microsoft Foundry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/microsoft-foundry.md). Requires Claude Code v2.1.203 or later |
| `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL` | Full base URL for the Microsoft Foundry resource (for example, `https://my-resource.services.ai.azure.com/anthropic`). Alternative to `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE` (see [Microsoft Foundry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/microsoft-foundry.md)) |
| `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE` | Microsoft Foundry resource name (for example, `my-resource`). Claude Code [refuses a URL or host name](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#anthropic-foundry-resource-must-be-a-foundry-resource-name). Required if `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL` is not set (see [Microsoft Foundry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/microsoft-foundry.md)) |
| `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` | Name of the model setting to use (see [Model Configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#environment-variables)) |
| `ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID` | Organization ID for [Workload Identity Federation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation). Set it together with `ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID`. See [authentication precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.md#authentication-precedence) |
| `ANTHROPIC_PROFILE` | Name of the Anthropic profile to authenticate with, such as one created by [`ant auth login`](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/cli/authentication) or by [signing in to a Console account without an API key](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.md#sign-in-without-an-api-key). See [authentication precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.md#authentication-precedence) |
| `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` | \[DEPRECATED] Name of [Haiku-class model for background tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs.md) |
| `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL_AWS_REGION` | Override AWS region for the Haiku-class model when using Amazon Bedrock or Amazon Bedrock Mantle. On Amazon Bedrock, this only takes effect when `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` or the deprecated `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` is also set, since Amazon Bedrock otherwise runs background tasks on the [default Sonnet model or the primary model](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/amazon-bedrock.md#4-pin-model-versions) in the session region |
| `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL` | Override Google Cloud's Agent Platform endpoint URL. Use for custom Google Cloud's Agent Platform endpoints or when routing through an [LLM gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway). See [Google Cloud's Agent Platform](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/google-vertex-ai.md) |
| `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID` | GCP project ID that Google Cloud's Agent Platform requests are addressed to. See [Configure GCP credentials](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/google-vertex-ai.md#3-configure-gcp-credentials) |
| `ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID` | Workspace ID for [workload identity federation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation). Set this when your federation rule is scoped to more than one workspace so the token exchange knows which workspace to target |
| `API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT` | Override the 5-minute body idle timeout that aborts a streaming model response when no bytes arrive. Set to `0` to turn the timeout off, for example when a slow [gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway) or local model pauses longer than 5 minutes between chunks, or `1` to keep it on for every provider. When unset, the timeout is active on providers other than the direct Anthropic API, [Claude Platform on AWS](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-platform-on-aws.md), and Amazon Bedrock with `CLAUDE_ENABLE_BYTE_WATCHDOG_BEDROCK=1` set. The [stream watchdogs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/network-config.md#streaming-idle-watchdogs) run independently of it and abort a long silent pause even when you set `0` here |
| `API_TIMEOUT_MS` | Time in milliseconds that each API request attempt has to receive its response headers. It doesn't limit how long a streaming response runs after that. The default is 600000, or 10 minutes, and the maximum is 2147483647. When you set a positive value, each attempt at a [non-streaming request](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#streaming-response-ended-before-any-complete-data-was-received) has to finish within it. Increase this when requests time out on slow networks or when routing through a proxy. Set to `0` to remove this limit, which requires Claude Code v2.1.305 or later. With `0`, a non-streaming attempt still times out after 300 seconds in a local session |
| `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` | Amazon Bedrock API key for authentication (see [Amazon Bedrock API keys](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerate-ai-development-with-amazon-bedrock-api-keys/)) |
| `BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` | Default timeout for a foreground Bash or PowerShell tool command, in milliseconds (default: 120000, or 2 minutes). A value above the [default time limit for background commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#time-limit-for-background-commands) replaces that default in unattended sessions. The background time limit requires Claude Code v2.1.285 or later |
| `BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH` | Maximum number of characters of bash output that Claude Code reads back into a command's result (default: 30000; maximum: 150000). If you set the [`bashOutputMaxChars`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#bashoutputmaxchars) setting, Claude Code ignores this variable. See [Output limits](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#output-limits) |
| `BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` | Maximum timeout the model can set for a foreground Bash or PowerShell tool command, in milliseconds (default: 600000, or 10 minutes). The effective ceiling is the larger of this and `BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`. An effective ceiling longer than 2 hours also becomes the maximum [time limit for background commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#time-limit-for-background-commands) in unattended sessions. The background time limit requires Claude Code v2.1.285 or later |
| `BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT` | OTLP/HTTP endpoint for [detailed beta tracing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage.md#traces-beta): with `ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED=1`, logs and traces go there instead of to the configured exporters. Set it in your shell, user settings, or managed settings. Ignored in [project and local settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env) |
| `CCR_FORCE_BUNDLE` | Set to `1` to force [`claude --cloud`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web#send-local-repositories-without-github) to bundle and upload your local repository instead of cloning from its remote |
| `CLAUDECODE` | Set to `1` in subprocesses Claude Code spawns (Bash and PowerShell tools, tmux sessions, [hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md) commands, [status line](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline.md) commands, stdio [MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md) subprocesses). IDE extensions also set this in their integrated terminals. Use to detect when a script is running inside a subprocess spawned by Claude Code. To check whether the current process was spawned directly by a tool call or hook, rather than inside a stdio MCP server that Claude Code started, use `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION` instead |
| `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS` | Set to `1` to disable all built-in [subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) types such as Explore and Plan. Only applies in non-interactive mode (the `-p` flag). Useful for SDK users who want a blank slate. This also removes `general-purpose`, the subagent Claude Code runs when an Agent tool call omits `subagent_type`. Such a call then fails with [`subagent_type is required`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors#subagent-type-is-required) |
| `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_MCP_NO_PREFIX` | Set to `1` to skip the `mcp__<server>__` prefix on tool names from SDK-created MCP servers. Tools use their original names. SDK usage only |
| `CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS` | Stall timeout in milliseconds for subagents. Also covers [workflow agents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md#when-an-agent-stalls-and-restarts) on Claude Code v2.1.286 or later. Default `600000` (10 minutes); if you raise `CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` while the stream watchdog is on, the default rises with it, as [Handle slow or stalled API responses](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript.md#handle-slow-or-stalled-api-responses) describes |
| `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE` | Set the percentage (1-100) of the auto-compact window at which auto-compaction triggers. Use lower values like `50` to compact earlier; the variable can't raise the threshold, so values above the default percentage are ignored. It applies only in sessions that [compact before the model's context limit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#context-window-and-auto-compaction). Applies to both main conversations and subagents |
| `CLAUDE_AUTO_BACKGROUND_TASKS` | Set to `1` to force-enable automatic backgrounding of long-running agent tasks. When enabled, a [subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background) moves to the background after running for approximately two minutes. If Claude queued a tool call such as a file edit behind the subagent, the subagent finishes in the foreground before that call starts. Also enables [automatic backgrounding of long MCP tool calls](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#automatic-backgrounding-of-long-tool-calls) in non-interactive mode on Claude Code v2.1.212 or later |
| `CLAUDE_AX_PREPARK_MS` | In [screen reader mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/accessibility.md), how many milliseconds Claude Code waits before it writes a new or changed line. Default `0`, so Claude Code doesn't wait. Before v2.1.287, the default was `50`. Claude Code caps the wait at `5000`. Ignored in [project and local settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env). Requires Claude Code v2.1.233 or later |
| `CLAUDE_AX_SCREEN_READER` | Set to `1` to render screen-reader friendly output: flat text without decorative borders or animations. Set to `0` to force screen-reader mode off even when [`axScreenReader`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#axscreenreader) is `true`. The [`--ax-screen-reader`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags) flag takes precedence. Ignored in [project and local settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env). Requires Claude Code v2.1.181 or later |
| `CLAUDE_AX_STARTUP_QUIET_MS` | In [screen reader mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/accessibility.md), how many milliseconds Claude Code holds the first interface render after the startup confirmation line. Your screen reader can then speak the line in full before new output interrupts it. Default `3000`. Set `0` to render immediately. Claude Code caps the hold at `600000` (10 minutes). Your first keystroke ends the hold early. Ignored in [project and local settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env). Requires Claude Code v2.1.217 or later |
| `CLAUDE_BASH_MAINTAIN_PROJECT_WORKING_DIR` | Return to the original working directory after each Bash or PowerShell command in the main session |
| `CLAUDE_BYTE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` | Timeout in milliseconds for the byte-level streaming idle watchdog; when set, it takes precedence over `CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` for that watchdog and leaves the event-level watchdog unchanged. Claude Code clamps this variable to between 10 seconds and 30 minutes. Requires Claude Code v2.1.210 or later |
| `CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE` | Path to a file that an external tool, such as a screen-lock listener, creates when you unlock your screen and deletes when you lock it. While the file exists, Claude Code skips [Remote Control mobile push notifications](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md#mobile-push-notifications), so you stop getting pushes while you are actively using the computer. When the file is absent or unreadable, notifications are sent as normal. Claude Code checks the file once per push-triggering event rather than polling it. Requires Claude Code v2.1.181 or later |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ACCESSIBILITY` | Set to `1` to keep the native terminal cursor visible and disable the inverted-text cursor indicator. Allows screen magnifiers like macOS Zoom to track cursor position |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD` | Set to `1` to load memory files from directories specified with `--add-dir`. Loads `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, and `CLAUDE.local.md`. By default, additional directories do not load memory files |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ALT_SCREEN_FULL_REPAINT` | Set to `1` to repaint the entire screen on every frame in [fullscreen rendering](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/fullscreen.md) instead of sending incremental updates. Use this if fullscreen mode shows stale or misplaced text fragments. Claude Code enables this automatically for background sessions and [agent view](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md) on Windows |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ALWAYS_ENABLE_EFFORT` | Set to `1` to send the [effort](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#adjust-effort-level) parameter with every request, even when Claude Code does not recognize the model ID as effort-capable. Use this when routing through an [LLM gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway) or third-party provider that serves models under custom identifiers. Models that reject the effort parameter at the API, including Claude Opus 4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and earlier models, are still excluded so requests do not fail |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_API_KEY_HELPER_TTL_MS` | Interval in milliseconds at which credentials should be refreshed (when using [`apiKeyHelper`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#apikeyhelper)) |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ARTIFACT_AUTO_OPEN` | Set to `0` to stop Claude Code from opening the browser automatically when a new [artifact](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/artifacts.md#create-an-artifact) is published |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ARTIFACT_COMMENTS` | Set to `0` to stop Claude reading and replying to [comments on an artifact](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/artifacts.md#collect-comments-on-an-artifact). Has no effect when `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` has [turned artifacts off](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/artifacts.md#availability). Requires Claude Code v2.1.221 or later |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ARTIFACT_COMMENTS_AUTOREACT` | Set to `0` to stop Claude [replying on its own to comments sent to it](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/artifacts.md#let-claude-reply-to-comments-on-its-own). Requires Claude Code v2.1.228 or later |

The settings page was read in full and has no MCP timeout keys.

**1. Tool-call timeout**
- **Default:** The MCP page summary says `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` falls back to "its default of about 28 hours when that variable is unset." Values below 1000 are ignored. The page doesn't state the unit, though the per-server example (`"timeout": 600000`, "ten minutes") implies milliseconds.
- **Per-server:** Add a `timeout` field "in milliseconds to that server's `.mcp.json` entry." Per the summary, it "overrides the `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` environment variable for that server only." Verbatim, the `ws` entry "accepts the same `url`, `headers`, `headersHelper`, `timeout`, and `alwaysLoad` fields as `http`."
- **Stdio:** The docs don't say whether `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` applies to stdio servers. The idle timeout (below) does cover stdio.
- **Plugins:** The docs don't say whether plugin-provided servers can set `timeout`.
- **Startup (separate):** `MCP_TIMEOUT` controls startup, e.g. `MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 claude`. Per the summary, it is also the floor for the HTTP per-request timer.
- **Idle timeout:** Per the env-vars summary, `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_TOOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (ms) aborts a call that sends "no response and no progress notification" for the window. Defaults are 300000 for network servers and 1800000 for stdio. Set `0` to disable.
- **Output size:** `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` defaults to 25,000 tokens (verbatim: "limits output to 25,000 tokens by default").

**2. Progress notifications**
- Summary, quoted: "The per-server `timeout` is a hard wall-clock limit per tool call, and progress notifications from the server don't extend it."
- Progress notifications do count as activity for the idle timer, since idle is defined as "no response and no progress notification." So they reset the idle timer but not the wall-clock limit.

**3. Esc and cancellation**
- The docs cover Esc only for MCP tasks: "pressing `Esc` or reaching the wall-clock limit or idle timeout ends the call, and Claude Code asks the server to cancel the task." Pressing Esc on a background task doesn't stop it.
- For an ordinary, non-task tool call, the docs are silent on whether the server is notified.

**4. Long-running and blocking calls**
- **Auto-backgrounding:** Per the summary, a call still running after two minutes "moves to a background task instead of blocking the session." Threshold is `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_AUTO_BACKGROUND_MS` (default 120000; `0` disables). It is off in non-interactive mode unless `CLAUDE_AUTO_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1`. Tasks don't survive exiting the session.
- **Waiting for user input (elicitation):** Per the summary, "A call waiting on an open elicitation dialog isn't backgrounded while the dialog is open." Declining or pressing Esc on that dialog is an answer to the server. In non-interactive mode, Claude Code asks the server to cancel a task that requests input.
- **Not covered:** The docs don't describe a tool that blocks waiting on something outside Claude Code, beyond elicitation.

Sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp (partial), https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars (partial), https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings (full).

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-12 18:25:10Z)**_

I'd separate two things here: the friction that's normal, and the one piece that could actually kill it.

**What's normal:** installing a plugin with two commands is how every Claude Code tool gets added. People will do that.

**What could kill it:** starting Claude Code every time with a long command that contains the word "dangerously". That's the only thing standing between a person and the map, and there may be a way around it.

**A way around it that needs testing.** Claude Code's MCP docs describe two behaviours that might add up to a push without a channel:
- A tool call that's still running after 2 minutes moves to the background, and you get your terminal back.
- A server can keep a call alive for a long time by sending regular progress updates (the idle limit for local servers is 30 minutes, reset by each update).

So illuminate could keep one tool call waiting for questions from the map. After 2 minutes it drops into the background and you carry on in the terminal. When you ask something on the map, the call returns with your question and Claude answers it.

If that works, setup becomes "install the plugin, run plain `claude`". There's no flag, and questions go to the same session that made the changes, which suits code review.

**What I don't know yet:**
- Some of this comes from summaries of the docs, not pages I read in full.
- Whether Claude actually starts working on its own when a backgrounded call finishes, as it does for background shell commands.
- What happens when you press Esc.

It's quick to settle. I'd add one waiting tool, and you'd press "Reconnect" for illuminate under `/mcp` in this session. I can then test it right here, because this session is connected to illuminate. It's about half an hour of work, and we'd know whether the flag can go.

**If it doesn't work, the options are:**
- Ask Anthropic for an official listing, which removes the flag. This is worth sending either way.
- Ask Anthropic whether illuminate may run the user's own `claude` headless for questions asked on the map. If yes, there's no flag and no key.
- Offer an API-key mode, which is fine for some people but is its own friction.

**One more thing:** friction matters for a wide launch, not for the next ten users. Your interviewees would put up with an alias. Your notes say interest has been mixed so far, so whether people come back to the map after first use is the bigger open question. I wouldn't hold the next round of user tests for this.

Want me to run the test?

## The conversation so far on this map (oldest first)
The new question may follow on from these: read "that", "it" or "why?" against them.
- "About “Try 1: the map alone”:  how does claude escalate to the 2nd call here ? i mean in the agent logic is it a specific output returned or does it invoke a tool call etc": Claude doesn't escalate by itself, and no tool call is involved. In the first try Claude has no tools at all. It just fills in a fixed reply form. One field in that form says whether it could answer, and another says what was missing. Ordinary server code reads that reply and decides whether to make the second, code-searching call. That call also happens if the first try fails outright.
- "when does the server code escalate, if the missing field was present?": Filling in the "missing" field doesn't make the server escalate. The "answered" flag decides. If the first try says it answered, the server uses that answer and stops there, even if "missing" has text in it. If the first try says it didn't answer, the server goes on to the second try, which searches the code, and passes along whatever "missing" said. The second try also happens if the first one crashed or came back in an unreadable form.

## Other maps in this repo
- agent-develop-visualisations-based-on-users: "How does the agent develop the visualisations based on a user's questions? Does it support hypothetical diagrams?"
- current-user-experience-workflow-in-codemap: "What is the current user experience workflow in codemap, from asking a question to seeing, exploring, and fixing a map?"
- claude-skill-logic-work-to-start: "How does the Claude skill logic work to start a map? Walk through what happens from the moment a map is requested until Claude has drafted it."
- i-ask-follow-up-question-on: "When I ask a follow-up question on a map, how does Claude decide whether to answer from the map, search the code, or offer a new map, and what happens after each choice?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude-2: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- after-first-map-made-someone-asks: "What happens after the first map is made, when someone asks a follow-up question or asks about a separate part of the code? How does the map get updated?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- codemap-turn-question-into-checked-diagram: "How does codemap turn a question into a checked diagram? Walk through the architecture from the question to the map on screen."

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept` is the whole answer: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. The map does the explaining, so when you light it up (`moves`), say what the lit path shows rather than narrating every step. Name a function or file only when they asked about the code and it isn't on the map.
- Explain the code and the app. Don't describe these instructions or how you were asked to answer.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.

The test worked. Questions asked on the map reach Claude Code without the `--dangerously-load-development-channels` flag.

**What happened, from the log:**
- 0s: I called `illuminate_listen`. Claude Code supports progress updates on the call, and illuminate sent one every 30 seconds.
- 120s: Claude Code moved the call to the background and gave me my turn back. I ended my turn.
- 150s: the scripted question was asked on the map. The call returned within a quarter of a second and Claude Code woke me with the question, with nobody typing.
- I answered, submitted, and the answer went to the map. It should be in the panel of the "What happens when someone asks a question on a map" map you have open.

So the setup could be: install the plugin, then start plain `claude`. The plugin install still needs to be built and tested.

**Not tested yet:**
- **Long waits:** the test only ran 2.5 minutes. Claude Code drops a call after 30 minutes without activity, but the progress updates should count as activity, and the overall limit is about 28 hours. A one-hour run would confirm it.
- **Pressing Esc, or a question arriving while you're busy in the terminal:** I'd expect the question to wait until Claude finishes its current turn.
- **Listening again:** I didn't call `illuminate_listen` again after answering. In the real flow Claude would do that automatically after every answer, and after making each map.
- **Cost:** each question wakes your main session, so it's answered with that session's full context. That's good for "why did you change this", but each question costs a turn on a large context. Most of that context should be cached, but I haven't measured it.

**To make it the real flow:**
1. After a map is made, and after every answer, Claude goes back to listening without being asked. I'd tell it to in the server's instructions, and `illuminate_submit` could also return straight into listening.
2. The channel push stays as a fallback for anyone who does start with the flag.
3. The README and skill lose the flag, and the start step becomes just `claude`.
4. Tests for the listen tool, and removing the test log.

The `illuminate_listen` tool and the test log in `packages/server/src/channel.ts` are still uncommitted test code. Should I turn this into the real flow?

    let s = servers.get(root);

        onStop: () => servers.delete(root),
        onEvent: (e) => void onEvent(root, e),

      servers.set(root, s);
    }
    return s;

  async function onEvent(root: string, e: ServerEvent) {

````text
## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate channel** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the user's
question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code, then
`illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Questions the user asks on the map
arrive later as illuminate channel messages; call `illuminate_next` for them. Don't edit files while working on a
request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open`
opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- As a Claude Code channel it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.
````

Listening is now the default flow in the code, and the docs no longer need the flag. All 51 server tests pass and the typecheck is clean. The full flow hasn't run in a live session yet; I've suggested a test at the end.

**How it works now**
- Once a map is ready, and after every answer, the server tells Claude to call `illuminate_listen` and leave it running. Claude Code moves the call to the background, and you get your terminal back. When you ask on the map, the call returns with your question and wakes the session.
- While a call waits, it sends a progress update every 30 seconds so Claude Code doesn't drop it as idle. This applies both to `illuminate_listen` and to the waits inside `illuminate_map` and `illuminate_submit`.
- If you press Esc, Claude Code cancels the call and the server stops listening cleanly. A question asked after that isn't lost: it waits, and the map says "Claude Code isn't listening to the map right now. In your Claude Code session, say 'listen to illuminate'". After 5 minutes it gives up.
- Starting Claude Code with the channel flag still works, but it's optional now. It only matters when nothing is listening.
- I removed the test log.

- Cancelling a listening call stops it, and a question asked afterwards still reaches Claude by the fallback route.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnzhang/.claude/skills/illuminate

# illuminate

illuminate turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that illuminate applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate MCP server** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the
user's question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code,
then `illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Once the map is ready, call
`illuminate_listen` and leave it running: it moves to the background, and returns with a request when the user asks
something on the map. Do it, submit it, and call `illuminate_listen` again. If the user says "listen to illuminate",
call `illuminate_listen`. Don't edit files while working on a request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a
sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open` opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- In Claude Code it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.

You make a map that answers a question about this codebase, for someone semi-technical. Explore with Read, Grep and Glob, then return the map as JSON. You cannot edit anything.

## The question
"how does our map generation process work, from searching the codebase to compiling?"

## What a good map is
- It follows what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job, a command) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API), or to where it stops.
- 2–6 `areas` named in product language (Patients, Billing, Background jobs), not folder names.
- 4–12 boxes (`nodes`). Each is one step a person would recognize. `name`: plain English, at most 30 characters ("Patient marked enrolled", not "markConverted()").
- `kind`: entry (a way in), step, store (table, queue, cache), external (outside service), job (scheduled or background work).
- `explain` for every box: just `concept`, 1–2 plain sentences, no jargon, saying what this step does. The box already shows its function and file, so leave those out.
- Arrow `label`: 1–3 words saying how one step leads to the next ("sends request", "calls", "announces", "every night").
- Code that exists but isn't reached from the start can still be boxes. Don't draw arrows that don't exist.
- An `absence` is a break in the flow you were asked about: a step on that path should lead to the next one and doesn't (something is announced that nothing listens for, a job that nothing ever starts). Most maps have none, and a map without one is complete. Don't go looking for one, and don't use one for a design choice or guarantee ("X never calls Y", "nothing here edits files"): say that in a box's explanation or the walkthrough instead. Don't record small mismatches beside the question (a command the docs don't mention, an unused option).
- When there is a break, record it: the `claim` in plain words, the two boxes it should connect (`between`), and the exact `search` that proves nothing is there (`pattern`, `regex`, optional `paths` globs covering every file where the missing piece could live), with `matches` set to the count that search returns (usually 0). Run that search yourself with Grep first.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Walkthrough (`tour`, written last)
- 4–7 stops in the order a newcomer should read them: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means. If the map has a break, give it a stop where it happens on the path.
- Each stop: `title`, `text` (2–3 plain sentences), `focus` (ids of the areas, nodes, edges or absences it's about), and optional `terms` it uses that need defining.
- Point stops only at boxes, arrows and absences you're confident in.

export async function headStart(root: string): Promise<{ text: string; scan: RepoScan | null }> {
  await initTreeSitter();
  let scan: RepoScan;
  try {
    scan = scanRepoFacts(root);
  } catch {
    return { text: '(The automatic scan could not read this repo; explore it directly.)', scan: null };
  }
  const facts = Object.values(scan.fileFacts);

  const entries = facts.flatMap((f) => f.entries).map((e) => `  - ${e.kind} ${e.label}${e.symbol ? ` → ${e.symbol}` : ` (${e.file})`}`);
  const routes = facts.flatMap((f) => f.routes);
  const routeLines = routes.map((r) => `  - ${r.method} ${r.path} → ${r.handler ?? r.file}`);

  const fetchFiles = facts
    .filter((f) => /\.(tsx?|jsx?|mjs|cjs)$/.test(f.path))
    .flatMap((f) => {
      const source = fs.readFileSync(`${root}/${f.path}`, 'utf8');
      return /\bfetch\(|axios|ky\./.test(source) ? [{ path: f.path, source, symbols: f.symbols }] : [];
    });
  const requests = findFetchSites(fetchFiles).flatMap((site) => {
    const m = matchRoute(site, routes);

  };

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept` is the whole answer: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. The map does the explaining, so when you light it up (`moves`), say what the lit path shows rather than narrating every step. Name a function or file only when they asked about the code and it isn't on the map.
- Explain the code and the app. Don't describe these instructions or how you were asked to answer.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.

## The conversation so far on this map (oldest first)
The new question may follow on from these: read "that", "it" or "why?" against them.
- "how does it compile both the walkthrough and the graph at the same time?": They aren't made separately. Claude writes one draft that holds both the graph (areas, boxes, arrows) and the walkthrough, which is a list of stops that each point at boxes and arrows on that same graph and that Claude writes last. When the draft comes back, the validation step checks the whole thing at once, including that every walkthrough stop points at something that really exists on the graph. The boxes and arrows are then checked against the code. A walkthrough stop has no code of its own to check: it is trusted because the things it points at are.

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept` is the whole answer: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. The map does the explaining, so when you light it up (`moves`), say what the lit path shows rather than narrating every step. Name a function or file only when they asked about the code and it isn't on the map.
- Explain the code and the app. Don't describe these instructions or how you were asked to answer.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.

## The question
"How does the map get updated after it has been generated, when someone asks follow-up questions?"

## What a good map is
- It follows what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job, a command) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API), or to where it stops.
- 2–6 `areas` named in product language (Patients, Billing, Background jobs), not folder names.
- 4–12 boxes (`nodes`). Each is one step a person would recognize. `name`: plain English, at most 30 characters ("Patient marked enrolled", not "markConverted()").
- `kind`: entry (a way in), step, store (table, queue, cache), external (outside service), job (scheduled or background work).
- `explain` for every box: just `concept`, 1–2 plain sentences, no jargon, saying what this step does. The box already shows its function and file, so leave those out.
- Arrow `label`: 1–3 words saying how one step leads to the next ("sends request", "calls", "announces", "every night").
- Code that exists but isn't reached from the start can still be boxes. Don't draw arrows that don't exist.
- An `absence` is a break in the flow you were asked about: a step on that path should lead to the next one and doesn't (something is announced that nothing listens for, a job that nothing ever starts). Most maps have none, and a map without one is complete. Don't go looking for one, and don't use one for a design choice or guarantee ("X never calls Y", "nothing here edits files"): say that in a box's explanation or the walkthrough instead. Don't record small mismatches beside the question (a command the docs don't mention, an unused option).
- When there is a break, record it: the `claim` in plain words, the two boxes it should connect (`between`), and the exact `search` that proves nothing is there (`pattern`, `regex`, optional `paths` globs covering every file where the missing piece could live), with `matches` set to the count that search returns (usually 0). Run that search yourself with Grep first.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Walkthrough (`tour`, written last)
- 4–7 stops in the order a newcomer should read them: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means. If the map has a break, give it a stop where it happens on the path.
- Each stop: `title`, `text` (2–3 plain sentences), `focus` (ids of the areas, nodes, edges or absences it's about), and optional `terms` it uses that need defining.
- Point stops only at boxes, arrows and absences you're confident in.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnzhang/.claude/skills/illuminate

# illuminate

illuminate turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that illuminate applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate MCP server** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the
user's question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code,
then `illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Once the map is ready, call
`illuminate_listen` and leave it running: it moves to the background, and returns with a request when the user asks
something on the map. Do it, submit it, and call `illuminate_listen` again. If the user says "listen to illuminate",
call `illuminate_listen`. Don't edit files while working on a request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a
sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open` opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- In Claude Code it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.

---
You make a map that answers a question about this codebase, for someone semi-technical. Explore with Read, Grep and Glob, then return the map as JSON. You cannot edit anything.

## The question
"how does my graph generation process work in the code with the agent?"

## What a good map is
- It follows what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job, a command) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API), or to where it stops.
- 2–6 `areas` named in product language (Patients, Billing, Background jobs), not folder names.
- 4–12 boxes (`nodes`). Each is one step a person would recognize. `name`: plain English, at most 30 characters ("Patient marked enrolled", not "markConverted()").
- `kind`: entry (a way in), step, store (table, queue, cache), external (outside service), job (scheduled or background work).
- `explain` for every box: just `concept`, 1–2 plain sentences, no jargon, saying what this step does. The box already shows its function and file, so leave those out.
- Arrow `label`: 1–3 words saying how one step leads to the next ("sends request", "calls", "announces", "every night").
- Code that exists but isn't reached from the start can still be boxes. Don't draw arrows that don't exist.
- An `absence` is a break in the flow you were asked about: a step on that path should lead to the next one and doesn't (something is announced that nothing listens for, a job that nothing ever starts). Most maps have none, and a map without one is complete. Don't go looking for one, and don't use one for a design choice or guarantee ("X never calls Y", "nothing here edits files"): say that in a box's explanation or the walkthrough instead. Don't record small mismatches beside the question (a command the docs don't mention, an unused option).
- When there is a break, record it: the `claim` in plain words, the two boxes it should connect (`between`), and the exact `search` that proves nothing is there (`pattern`, `regex`, optional `paths` globs covering every file where the missing piece could live), with `matches` set to the count that search returns (usually 0). Run that search yourself with Grep first.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Walkthrough (`tour`, written last)
- 4–7 stops in the order a newcomer should read them: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means. If the map has a break, give it a stop where it happens on the path.
- Each stop: `title`, `text` (2–3 plain sentences), `focus` (ids of the areas, nodes, edges or absences it's about), and optional `terms` it uses that need defining.
- Point stops only at boxes, arrows and absences you're confident in.

Mostly yes. Questions asked on the map reach your session without the channel flag. But that background listening call just broke after 30 minutes: Claude Code dropped it with "sent no response or progress for 1841s". It didn't count the progress updates illuminate sends every 30 seconds as activity, at least once the call was in the background. So right now, after half an hour of quiet, the next question on the map gets the "Claude Code isn't listening" notice.

**The fix:** the listening call returns on its own just before 30 minutes, and Claude starts a new one. Each restart costs one short turn on your session. I'd stop after about two hours of no questions so it doesn't run all night. I'd also set a longer per-server timeout in the install config, which the error message itself suggests. That's under an hour of work, and I can do it next.

**What I took from Edward**
- **His pain is a big monorepo that no one understands as a whole, and a QA bottleneck.** He wants sales and product people to understand how things work without asking him. That's a different buyer from the solo builders: a team lead who wants understanding spread across the team.
- **The use is sharing:** onboarding, understanding a long piece of agent work, and explaining things to non-technical people. This matches Adam (onboarding) and Divam (reviewing changes before they reach production). Three people independently landed on "send this to someone else".
- **Showing the frontend grounds the backend for non-technical people,** and he has already built this himself: onboarding videos made from one prompt, with a recorded interface and fake Slack and email. He was clear that it should still explain how things work technically.

**Frontend grounding: what I'd build**
- **Screen boxes from the component code.** Entry points already know where they start, for example "the Convert button in the patient header sends POST /convert". A screen box would show a small wireframe of that part of the screen, built from the component's own markup (button labels, fields, headings), and the walkthrough would begin there: "you press Convert, and this happens". Like every other claim, the button label is a cited line the checker can confirm. It's low-fidelity, but it's true and cheap.
- **Real screenshots, later.** Illuminate could drive the running app and capture each screen. It looks better, but needs the app running, logins and test data, so it's much heavier.
- **Claude-drawn mockups are what I'd avoid.** They look like the product but nothing checks them, which goes against the core rule that nothing on screen is unchecked.
- **The "video":** the walkthrough already moves the camera stop by stop and shows text at each stop. An autoplay mode with an optional voiceover, starting on the screen, is most of Edward's three-minute video without making an actual video file.

**Sharing: from cheapest to most involved**
1. **One self-contained HTML file per map:** the map, walkthrough and explanations, with no server and no key. You'd drop it in Slack or attach it to a PR. Anyone can explore it and take the walkthrough, but they can't ask new questions, and it's stamped with the commit it was checked at. This covers onboarding and change review at almost no cost. One catch: the file includes the cited lines of code, so it's as sensitive as the code itself.
2. **A map of a pull request, posted on the PR,** as that same file or a link. This is Divam's case and turns illuminate into a code review tool.
3. **Hosted maps that teammates can ask questions on.** This needs a server with access to the repo and an API key, which makes it a real product (likely a GitHub app) with privacy questions for teams working on production code. I'd only build it once the shared files show people actually open them.

**What I'd do in order:**
1. Fix the 30-minute listening problem.
2. The shareable HTML file.
3. Screen boxes for entry points.
4. Autoplay walkthrough.

The shareable file is the fastest way to test Edward's sharing idea with real teams: send one to him and see whether his team opens it.
