import { inOverview, overviewOf } from '../src/overview';

const APP = fileURLToPath(new URL('../../core/test/fixtures/care-app', import.meta.url));
const json = JSON.parse(readFileSync(fileURLToPath(new URL('../../core/test/fixtures/care-app.map.json', import.meta.url)), 'utf8'));
const parsed = parseMap(json);
if (!parsed.ok) throw new Error(parsed.problems.join('\n'));
const map = parsed.map;
const report = check(map, APP);

describe('the big picture', () => {
  const o = overviewOf(map, report);

  it('has one box per area, named after it, standing for the steps inside', () => {
    expect(o.map.nodes.map((n) => n.name)).toEqual(map.areas.map((a) => a.label));
    expect(o.map.nodes).toHaveLength(map.areas.length);
    const patients = o.map.nodes.find((n) => n.id === 'ov.patients')!;
    expect(patients.kind).toBe('entry');
    expect(o.inside['ov.patients']).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining(map.nodes.filter((n) => n.area === 'patients').map((n) => n.id)));
  });

  it('draws one numbered arrow per pair of areas, only where a real arrow crosses, and keeps the missing connection', () => {
    const areaOf = new Map(map.nodes.map((n) => [n.id, n.area]));
    const crossing = new Set(map.edges.filter((e) => areaOf.get(e.from) !== areaOf.get(e.to)).map((e) => `${areaOf.get(e.from)}>${areaOf.get(e.to)}`));
    expect(o.map.edges).toHaveLength(crossing.size);
    o.map.edges.forEach((e, i) => expect(e.label.startsWith(`${i + 1} · `)).toBe(true));
    expect(o.map.absences).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(o.map.absences[0]!.between).toEqual({ from: 'ov.events', to: 'ov.automations' });
  });

  it('is confirmed only where everything inside is, and lights the boxes that stand for what a stop lights', () => {
    expect(Object.values(o.report!.nodes).every((c) => c.status === 'confirmed')).toBe(true);
    const broken = structuredClone(report);
    broken.nodes[map.nodes[0]!.id]!.status = 'unconfirmed';
    expect(overviewOf(map, broken).report!.nodes[`ov.${map.nodes[0]!.area}`]!.status).toBe('unconfirmed');
    expect(inOverview(o, [map.nodes[0]!.id, 'miss', 'nope'])).toEqual([`ov.${map.nodes[0]!.area}`, o.map.absences[0]!.id]);
  });
});

export function makerPrompt(question: string, headStart: string): string {
  return [
    'You make a map that answers a question about this codebase, for someone semi-technical. Explore with Read, Grep and Glob, then return the map as JSON. You cannot edit anything.',

    '',
    '## Head start (from a quick automatic scan; it may be incomplete)',
    headStart,
    '',
    'Return the map: `version` 1, the `question`, `areas`, `nodes`, `edges`, `absences`, `tour`.',
  ].join('\n');
}

export function shapeRepairPrompt(problems: readonly string[]): string {
  return [
    'The map you returned has problems that stop it from being drawn:',
    ...problems.map((p) => `- ${p}`),
    '',
    'Return the complete corrected map.',
  ].join('\n');
}

/** What a repair prompt needs to suggest real names: the function names the code facts know in a file. */
export type SymbolsIn = (file: string) => readonly string[];

const NO_SYMBOL = /^the code has no symbol (.+)#(.+)$/;
/** "the code has no symbol a.ts#save" → the same reason, plus the names in a.ts that end in `save` (or a few names). */
function withSuggestion(reason: string, symbolsIn: SymbolsIn | undefined): string {
  const m = NO_SYMBOL.exec(reason);
  if (!m || !symbolsIn) return reason;
  const [, file, name] = m as unknown as [string, string, string];
  const last = name.split('.').at(-1)!;
  const names = symbolsIn(file);
  const close = names.filter((n) => n === last || n.endsWith(`.${last}`));
  if (close.length) return `${reason} (in that file it's ${close.slice(0, 3).map((n) => `${file}#${n}`).join(' or ')})`;
  return names.length ? `${reason} (that file has: ${names.slice(0, 12).join(', ')})` : reason;
}

export function evidenceRepairPrompt(report: CheckReport, symbolsIn?: SymbolsIn): string {
  const why = (reasons: string[]) => reasons.map((r) => withSuggestion(r, symbolsIn)).join('; ');
  const lines = [
    ...Object.entries(report.nodes).filter(([, c]) => c.status !== 'confirmed').map(([id, c]) => `- box ${id}: ${why(c.reasons)}`),
    ...Object.entries(report.edges).filter(([, c]) => c.status !== 'confirmed').map(([id, c]) => `- arrow ${id}: ${why(c.reasons)}`),
    ...Object.entries(report.absences).filter(([, c]) => c.status !== 'confirmed').map(([id, c]) => `- absence ${id}: ${c.reasons.join('; ')}${c.locations.length ? ` (found at ${c.locations.slice(0, 5).map((l) => `${l.file}:${l.line}`).join(', ')})` : ''}`),
  ];
  const screens = Object.entries(report.screens ?? {}).filter(([, c]) => c.status !== 'confirmed').map(([id, c]) => `- screen on box ${id}: ${c.reasons.join('; ')}`);
  return [
    'The checker re-read the code and could not confirm these claims:',
    ...lines,
    ...(screens.length ? ['', 'These screens can\'t be shown either (fix the `screen` on the box, or return the box without it):', ...screens] : []),
    '',
    'Fix only these. For each one, correct it (exact line text, right line number, a real symbol name, the right arrow kind) or drop it if it isn\'t true. If an absence was wrong, the code is connected after all: drop the absence and add that arrow.',
    '',
    'Return only the changes, not the whole map. Put each corrected box, arrow or absence (complete, with all its fields and the same id) and anything new in `nodes`, `edges`, `absences` or `areas`, and the ids of claims to drop in `remove`. Everything you leave out stays as it is.',
  ].join('\n');
}

export function patchRepairPrompt(problems: readonly string[]): string {
  return [
    'Your changes couldn\'t be applied to the map:',
    ...problems.map((p) => `- ${p}`),
    '',
    'Return the corrected changes, in the same form: only what changes, each item complete.',
  ].join('\n');
}

export type SelectionLine = { id: string; label: string };

/** The map, what the checker couldn't confirm, what they selected and their question: shared by both answer prompts. */
function questionContext(map: CodeMap, report: CheckReport, selection: readonly SelectionLine[], question: string): string[] {
  const unconfirmed = [
    ...Object.entries(report.nodes), ...Object.entries(report.edges), ...Object.entries(report.absences),
  ].filter(([, c]) => c.status !== 'confirmed').map(([id]) => id);
  return [
    '## The map (JSON)',
    JSON.stringify(map),
    unconfirmed.length ? `\nThe checker could not confirm: ${unconfirmed.join(', ')}. Don\'t rely on those without checking.` : '\nThe checker confirmed every claim in the map.',
    '',
    selection.length ? `## They selected\n${selection.map((s) => `- ${s.id}: ${s.label}`).join('\n')}` : '## They selected nothing (the question is about the whole map)',
    '',
    `## Their question\n"${question}"`,
  ];
}

/** A turn of the conversation on a map, as the next answer sees it. */
export type EarlierTurn = { question: string; concept: string };

/** The conversation so far, oldest first, so a follow-up ("show me that in the code") knows what "that" is. */
function conversationSoFar(earlier: readonly EarlierTurn[]): string[] {
  if (!earlier.length) return [];
  return [
    '## The conversation so far on this map (oldest first)',
    'The new question may follow on from these: read "that", "it" or "why?" against them.',
    ...earlier.map((e) => `- "${e.question}": ${e.concept}`),

// What the model must return, as JSON Schema for structured output. Derived from the map format's zod schemas, so the
// two can't drift. Output is still validated with zod (and the map with `parseMap`) after it comes back.
import { z } from 'zod';
import { Absence, Area, CodeMap, Edge, Node, Screen } from '@illuminate/core';

/** Keywords some structured-output validators reject; zod and `parseMap` enforce them after the fact anyway. */
const STRIP = new Set(['$schema', '$id', 'pattern', 'default', 'format']);

function sanitize(value: unknown): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(sanitize);
  if (!value || typeof value !== 'object') return value;
  const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(value)) if (!STRIP.has(k)) out[k] = sanitize(v);
  return out;
}

export function toSchema(schema: z.ZodType): Record<string, unknown> {
  return sanitize(z.toJSONSchema(schema, { io: 'input' })) as Record<string, unknown>;
}

export const RawFix = z.object({
  summary: z.string().min(1).max(600),
  /** Exact-text replacements: `find` is copied from the file and occurs exactly once. */
  edits: z.array(z.object({ file: z.string().min(1), find: z.string().min(1), replace: z.string() })).max(12).default([]),
  creates: z.array(z.object({ file: z.string().min(1), content: z.string() })).max(6).default([]),
  /** The connection the fix creates between two boxes; `evidenceText` must appear in the new code. */
  connects: z
    .object({ from: z.string(), to: z.string(), label: z.string().min(1).max(60), evidenceFile: z.string().min(1), evidenceText: z.string().min(1).max(200) })
    .optional(),
});

/**
 * A box as Claude writes it: the map format's node, but only the plain explanation. The format still allows `how` and
 * `code` (older maps have them), but the map shows the code itself, so Claude isn't asked for them.
 */
const WrittenNode = Node.extend({ explain: z.object({ concept: z.string() }).partial().optional() });

/** The map as Claude writes it (see `WrittenNode`); read back with `parseMap` against the full format. */
const WrittenMap = CodeMap.extend({ nodes: z.array(WrittenNode).min(1) });

export const RawAnswer = z.object({
  /** The answer, as short Markdown shaped to the question (see `ANSWER_STYLE`). The map does the explaining; this says what's lit. */
  concept: z.string().min(1),
  /** Ids of the boxes, arrows and missing connections the answer relies on. */
  refs: z.array(z.string()).default([]),
  /** New things found while exploring, with evidence, same rules as the map. */
  add: z
    .object({ areas: z.array(Area).optional(), nodes: z.array(WrittenNode).optional(), edges: z.array(Edge).optional(), absences: z.array(Absence).optional() })
    .optional(),
  moves: z.object({ focus: z.string().optional(), highlight: z.array(z.string()).optional() }).optional(),

The guidelines for what a map should look like are short: about ten lines in `packages/server/src/prompts.ts:13`. Most of the prompt goes to evidence and missing connections rather than to making the map easy to read.

## What Claude is told today

**The map**
- **Shape:** follow what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API).
- **Areas:** 2–6, named in product language ("Billing"), not folder names.
- **Boxes:** 4–12, each "one step a person would recognize", with a plain-English name of at most 30 characters.
- **Box kinds:** entry, step, store, external or job.
- **Box explanation:** 1–2 plain sentences on what the step does.
- **Arrow labels:** 1–3 words on how one step leads to the next ("calls", "announces", "every night").
- **Missing connections:** only a real break in the flow that was asked about, with the search that proves it. Most maps should have none.

**Evidence**
- Every box and arrow cites an exact line.
- Function names must match the checker's.
- An arrow's kind (`calls`, `request`, `imports`) is used only when literally true.

**Screens**
- Optional and Claude's call, one or two per map at most.

**Walkthrough**
- 4–7 stops of 2–3 sentences each: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means.

## Where I think it falls short

1. **Nothing sets the level of a box.** "One step a person would recognize" is the only rule. It doesn't say to fold helpers, validation and logging into the step they serve, or that a box is not a function. This is the gap behind your abstraction worry, and tightening it is cheaper than a second view.
2. **Arrow labels say how, not what.** The prompt's own example is "calls", which tells a reader nothing. "Sends the order" or "saves the result" would carry the story.
3. **The size limits are only suggestions.** The format accepts names up to 80 characters, labels up to 60 and any number of boxes. A 20-box map passes with no complaint.
4. **No main path.** Nothing tells Claude to pick one spine and keep branches and error cases to the few that matter for the question, so maps can sprawl sideways.
5. **The question isn't answered anywhere.** No rule says the first walkthrough stop should answer the question in a sentence. "What the map shows" tends to produce a description of the map instead.
6. **Explanations don't tie back to the question.** They say what a step does, not why it matters here.

## What I'd change

I'd change 1, 2 and 5 in the prompt, and have the code send a map back for one repair round when it runs over the box or name limits (3). They're small edits, but you'd need to regenerate a map or two to judge them.

Do you want me to make those four, or would you rather edit the wording yourself first?

# illuminate

illuminate turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that illuminate applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate MCP server** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the
user's question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code,
then `illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Once the map is ready, call
`illuminate_listen` and leave it running: it moves to the background, and returns with a request when the user asks
something on the map. Do it, submit it, and call `illuminate_listen` again. If it returns saying nothing was asked yet,
call it again without mentioning it; if it says illuminate stopped listening, don't. If the user says "listen to
illuminate", call `illuminate_listen`. Don't edit files while working on a request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a
sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open` opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- In Claude Code it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.

You make a map that answers a question about this codebase, for someone semi-technical. Explore with Read, Grep and Glob, then return the map as JSON. You cannot edit anything.

## The question
"how does claude currently generate the map guidelines wise, from search to generating something interpretable?"

## What a good map is
- It follows what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job, a command) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API), or to where it stops.
- 2–6 `areas` named in product language (Patients, Billing, Background jobs), not folder names.
- 4–12 boxes (`nodes`). Each is one step a person would recognize. `name`: plain English, at most 30 characters ("Patient marked enrolled", not "markConverted()").
- `kind`: entry (a way in), step, store (table, queue, cache), external (outside service), job (scheduled or background work).
- `explain` for every box: just `concept`, 1–2 plain sentences, no jargon, saying what this step does. The box already shows its function and file, so leave those out.
- Arrow `label`: 1–3 words saying how one step leads to the next ("sends request", "calls", "announces", "every night").
- Code that exists but isn't reached from the start can still be boxes. Don't draw arrows that don't exist.
- An `absence` is a break in the flow you were asked about: a step on that path should lead to the next one and doesn't (something is announced that nothing listens for, a job that nothing ever starts). Most maps have none, and a map without one is complete. Don't go looking for one, and don't use one for a design choice or guarantee ("X never calls Y", "nothing here edits files"): say that in a box's explanation or the walkthrough instead. Don't record small mismatches beside the question (a command the docs don't mention, an unused option).
- When there is a break, record it: the `claim` in plain words, the two boxes it should connect (`between`), and the exact `search` that proves nothing is there (`pattern`, `regex`, optional `paths` globs covering every file where the missing piece could live), with `matches` set to the count that search returns (usually 0). Run that search yourself with Grep first.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Screens (`screen` on a box; optional, and your call)
- A picture of what the person sees can ground a map for people who don't read code. Add one where the flow touches the screen and seeing it helps: usually the box where it starts (the button or form), sometimes where a result appears. For backend-only questions, add none. One or two per map is plenty.
- `{ "kind": "capture", "capture": "<id>", "highlight": "<label>" }`: a real screenshot. Only if you have the illuminate_capture tool: it screenshots a page already running on this machine or an HTML file in the repo, and returns the id. Look at the image first, and don't use one that shows a login page, an error or the wrong state. Never start the app yourself.
- `{ "kind": "image", "file": "<path>" }`: an image file in the repo (an icon, a sprite) that the box's cited code names.
- `{ "kind": "sketch", "file": "<markup file>", "elements": [{ "kind": "heading|button|field|link|text|image", "text": "…" }], "highlight": "<one element's text>" }`: a rough wireframe of the visible things in a component or template, top to bottom, at most 12. Use it when there is no screenshot to take. Copy each `text` exactly from the file.
- A program checks screens too: a capture's `highlight` must be a label visible on it and appear in the code the box cites; every sketch element must be in its file. A screen that fails is left out; the box stays.

## Walkthrough (`tour`, written last)
- 4–7 stops in the order a newcomer should read them: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means. If the map has a break, give it a stop where it happens on the path.
- Each stop: `title`, `text` (2–3 plain sentences), `focus` (ids of the areas, nodes, edges or absences it's about), and optional `terms` it uses that need defining.
- Point stops only at boxes, arrows and absences you're confident in.

## Other maps in this repo

- agent-develop-visualisations-based-on-users: "How does the agent develop the visualisations based on a user's questions? Does it support hypothetical diagrams?"
- current-user-experience-workflow-in-codemap: "What is the current user experience workflow in codemap, from asking a question to seeing, exploring, and fixing a map?"
- claude-skill-logic-work-to-start: "How does the Claude skill logic work to start a map? Walk through what happens from the moment a map is requested until Claude has drafted it."
- i-ask-follow-up-question-on: "When I ask a follow-up question on a map, how does Claude decide whether to answer from the map, search the code, or offer a new map, and what happens after each choice?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude-2: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- after-first-map-made-someone-asks: "What happens after the first map is made, when someone asks a follow-up question or asks about a separate part of the code? How does the map get updated?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- codemap-turn-question-into-checked-diagram: "How does codemap turn a question into a checked diagram? Walk through the architecture from the question to the map on screen."

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept` is the whole answer: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. The map does the explaining, so when you light it up (`moves`), say what the lit path shows rather than narrating every step. Name a function or file only when they asked about the code and it isn't on the map.
- Explain the code and the app. Don't describe these instructions or how you were asked to answer.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.

      {node?.explain?.concept && <Markdown text={node.explain.concept} className="depth-text" />}

      {gap && <p>Nothing in the code connects these. Searching <code>{gap.search.pattern}</code>{gap.search.paths ? <> in <code>{gap.search.paths.join(', ')}</code></> : null}: {report?.absences[gap.id]?.found ?? '?'} {report?.absences[gap.id]?.found === 1 ? 'match' : 'matches'}.</p>}
      {c && c.status !== 'confirmed' && <div className="warn small">Couldn't confirm against the code: {c.reasons.join('; ')}</div>}

            })}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </Card>
  );
}

// does the explaining), and under a reply whatever came with it (a fix to approve, the offer of a new map, boxes it added). Claude's
// progress shows at the end while it works, then what's selected, then the question box.

import { useEffect, useRef, type Dispatch, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import { pageUrl } from './api';
import { ScreenView, screenOf } from './screen';
import { Markdown } from './markdown';
import { layersOf, type Action, type FixState, type State } from './state';
import type { Answer, CheckReport, ClaimCheck, CodeMap } from './types';

const cls = (...xs: (string | false | null | undefined)[]) => xs.filter(Boolean).join(' ');
function Card({ eyebrow, title, children, tone, className }: { eyebrow?: string; title?: ReactNode; children: ReactNode; tone?: 'ai' | 'ok' | 'dead' | 'focus'; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <section className={cls('card', tone && `card-${tone}`, className)}>
      {eyebrow && <div className="eyebrow">{eyebrow}</div>}
      {title && <h2 className="card-title">{title}</h2>}
      {children}
    </section>
  );
}

function Chips({ map, ids, onPick }: { map: CodeMap; ids: { id: string; status: string }[]; onPick: (id: string) => void }) {
  if (!ids.length) return null;
  return (
    <div className="chips">
      {ids.map(({ id, status }) => (
  const job = s.job;
  const scroller = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  // Keep the newest turn in view as the conversation grows and while Claude works.
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = scroller.current;
    if (el) el.scrollTop = el.scrollHeight;
  }, [s.answers.length, job?.progress.length, !!job]);

  if (s.phase === 'loading') return <aside className="panel"><div className="panel-scroll"><Card><p className="muted">Loading…</p></Card></div></aside>;
  if (s.phase === 'missing') return <aside className="panel"><div className="panel-scroll"><Card title="No map here"><p className="muted">This map isn't in this repo.</p></Card></div></aside>;
  if (!map) {
    return (
      <aside className="panel">
        <div className="panel-scroll">
          {job && (
            <Card eyebrow="Making your map" title={job.question} tone="ai">
              <Progress lines={job.progress} working />
            </Card>
          )}
          {s.phase === 'failed' && <Card title="The map couldn't be made" tone="dead"><p>{s.error}</p></Card>}
        </div>
      </aside>
    );
  }

  const selected = [...s.selection.nodes, ...s.selection.edges, ...s.selection.absences];
  const layers = layersOf(s);
  const allHidden = layers.length > 0 && layers.every((l) => !l.visible);

  return (
    <aside className="panel" aria-label="Conversation about this map">
      <header className="panel-head">
        <h2 className="panel-title">Conversation</h2>
        {layers.length > 0 && (
          <button className="link-btn small" onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'allLayers', visible: allHidden })}>{allHidden ? 'Show everything' : 'Show the original map'}</button>
        )}
        <button className="card-close" aria-label="Close the conversation" title="Close (Esc). It stays here to reopen." onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'overview' })}>×</button>
      </header>

      <div className="panel-scroll" ref={scroller}>
        {s.error && <div className="banner banner-dead" role="alert">{s.error}<button className="link-btn" onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'error', message: null })}>Dismiss</button></div>}

        {s.answers.map((a) => (
          <Turn key={a.id} answer={a} state={s} dispatch={dispatch} onFix={onFix} onFocus={onFocus} onOffer={onOffer} />
        ))}

        {job?.kind === 'ask' && (
          <article className="turn">
            <You question={job.question} />
            <Card eyebrow="Claude is working" tone="ai">
              <Progress lines={job.progress} working />
            </Card>
          </article>
        )}

        {!s.answers.length && !job && !selected.length && <p className="muted small thread-empty">Ask anything about this map. Click a box or arrow first to ask about it.</p>}
      </div>

      <footer className="panel-foot">
        {selected.length > 0 && <Selected map={map} report={s.report} ids={selected} />}
        {composer}
      </footer>
    </aside>
  );
}

# illuminate

illuminate turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that illuminate applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

**In Claude Code with the illuminate MCP server** (you have an `illuminate_map` tool): call `illuminate_map` with the
user's question in their own words. It opens the map in their browser and hands you work as requests: explore the code,
then `illuminate_submit` your output. Keep going while results hold another request. Once the map is ready, call
`illuminate_listen` and leave it running: it moves to the background, and returns with a request when the user asks
something on the map. Do it, submit it, and call `illuminate_listen` again. If it returns saying nothing was asked yet,
call it again without mentioning it; if it says illuminate stopped listening, don't. If the user says "listen to
illuminate", call `illuminate_listen`. Don't edit files while working on a request, and keep what you say in the terminal to a
sentence or two: the map does the explaining. `illuminate_open` opens saved maps.

**Otherwise**, run the CLI from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). It needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`:

```bash
illume "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last illuminate tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop illuminate on the page. If an illuminate server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `illume list` prints the maps already made in this repo (saved under `.illuminate/maps/`), one `<map-id>  <question>`
  per line. Use it to find a map's id, or to check whether a map for the question already exists.
- `illume open [<map-id>]` opens those maps in the user's browser (one map, or the list of all of them).
- `illume check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- illuminate reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- In Claude Code it uses the session it runs in, so no key. The CLI needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If `illume` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the illuminate repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.

## The question
"what are the guidelines/criteria we use to generate maps"

## What a good map is
- It follows what happens, in order, from where it starts (a button, a route, a job, a command) to where it ends (a table write, an email, an outside API), or to where it stops.
- 2–6 `areas` named in product language (Patients, Billing, Background jobs), not folder names.
- 4–12 boxes (`nodes`). Each is one step a person would recognize. `name`: plain English, at most 30 characters ("Patient marked enrolled", not "markConverted()").
- `kind`: entry (a way in), step, store (table, queue, cache), external (outside service), job (scheduled or background work).
- `explain` for every box: just `concept`, 1–2 plain sentences, no jargon, saying what this step does. The box already shows its function and file, so leave those out.
- Arrow `label`: 1–3 words saying how one step leads to the next ("sends request", "calls", "announces", "every night").
- Code that exists but isn't reached from the start can still be boxes. Don't draw arrows that don't exist.
- An `absence` is a break in the flow you were asked about: a step on that path should lead to the next one and doesn't (something is announced that nothing listens for, a job that nothing ever starts). Most maps have none, and a map without one is complete. Don't go looking for one, and don't use one for a design choice or guarantee ("X never calls Y", "nothing here edits files"): say that in a box's explanation or the walkthrough instead. Don't record small mismatches beside the question (a command the docs don't mention, an unused option).
- When there is a break, record it: the `claim` in plain words, the two boxes it should connect (`between`), and the exact `search` that proves nothing is there (`pattern`, `regex`, optional `paths` globs covering every file where the missing piece could live), with `matches` set to the count that search returns (usually 0). Run that search yourself with Grep first.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Screens (`screen` on a box; optional, and your call)
- A picture of what the person sees can ground a map for people who don't read code. Add one where the flow touches the screen and seeing it helps: usually the box where it starts (the button or form), sometimes where a result appears. For backend-only questions, add none. One or two per map is plenty.
- `{ "kind": "capture", "capture": "<id>", "highlight": "<label>" }`: a real screenshot. Only if you have the illuminate_capture tool: it screenshots a page already running on this machine or an HTML file in the repo, and returns the id. Look at the image first, and don't use one that shows a login page, an error or the wrong state. Never start the app yourself.
- `{ "kind": "image", "file": "<path>" }`: an image file in the repo (an icon, a sprite) that the box's cited code names.
- `{ "kind": "sketch", "file": "<markup file>", "elements": [{ "kind": "heading|button|field|link|text|image", "text": "…" }], "highlight": "<one element's text>" }`: a rough wireframe of the visible things in a component or template, top to bottom, at most 12. Use it when there is no screenshot to take. Copy each `text` exactly from the file.
- A program checks screens too: a capture's `highlight` must be a label visible on it and appear in the code the box cites; every sketch element must be in its file. A screen that fails is left out; the box stays.

## Walkthrough (`tour`, written last)
- 4–7 stops in the order a newcomer should read them: what the map shows, then the path, then what it means. If the map has a break, give it a stop where it happens on the path.
- Each stop: `title`, `text` (2–3 plain sentences), `focus` (ids of the areas, nodes, edges or absences it's about), and optional `terms` it uses that need defining.
- Point stops only at boxes, arrows and absences you're confident in.

function checkEdge(e: MapEdge, byId: ReadonlyMap<string, MapNode>, repo: RepoReader, facts: Facts, window: number): ClaimCheck {
  const evidence = e.evidence.map((x) => checkEvidence(repo, x, window));
  const reasons = evidenceReasons(evidence);
  const from = byId.get(e.from);
  const to = byId.get(e.to);
  if (reasons.length || !from || !to || e.kind === 'then') return result(evidence, reasons, 'text');

  if (e.kind === 'calls') {
    if (!from.symbol || !to.symbol) return result(evidence, reasons, 'text');
    const calls = facts.calls(fileOf(from.symbol), [fileOf(to.symbol)]);
    if (!calls.some((c) => within(c.from, from.symbol!) && c.to === to.symbol)) reasons.push(`the code has no call from ${from.symbol} to ${to.symbol}`);
    return result(evidence, reasons, 'fact');
  }

  const fromFile = from.symbol ? fileOf(from.symbol) : from.evidence[0]!.file;
  const toFile = to.symbol ? fileOf(to.symbol) : to.evidence[0]!.file;
  const fromFacts = facts.get(fromFile);
  if (!fromFacts) {
    reasons.push(`${fromFile} can't be read`);
    return result(evidence, reasons, 'fact');
  }

  if (e.kind === 'imports') {
    if (!fromFacts.imports.some((i) => i.to === toFile)) reasons.push(`${fromFile} doesn't import ${toFile}`);
    return result(evidence, reasons, 'fact');
  }

  // request: a fetch in the `from` box (direct, or through a wrapper it imports) that matches a route in the `to` box.
  const neighbours = [fromFile, ...fromFacts.imports.filter((i) => !i.to.startsWith('vendor:')).map((i) => i.to)];
  const sources = neighbours.flatMap((path) => {
    const source = repo.text(path);
    const f = facts.get(path);
    return source !== null && f ? [{ path, source, symbols: f.symbols }] : [];
  });
  const routes = facts.get(toFile)?.routes ?? [];
  const matched = findFetchSites(sources).some((site) => {
    if (site.file !== fromFile || (from.symbol && !within(site.from, from.symbol))) return false;
    const m = matchRoute(site, routes);
    return !!m && (to.symbol ? m.route.handler === to.symbol : true);
  });
  if (!matched) reasons.push(`no request from ${from.symbol ?? fromFile} matches a route handled by ${to.symbol ?? toFile}`);
  return result(evidence, reasons, 'fact');
}

- our-map-generation-process-work-from: "how does our map generation process work, from searching the codebase to compiling?"

- agent-develop-visualisations-based-on-users: "How does the agent develop the visualisations based on a user's questions? Does it support hypothetical diagrams?"

- i-ask-follow-up-question-on: "When I ask a follow-up question on a map, how does Claude decide whether to answer from the map, search the code, or offer a new map, and what happens after each choice?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude-2: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- after-first-map-made-someone-asks: "What happens after the first map is made, when someone asks a follow-up question or asks about a separate part of the code? How does the map get updated?"
- explain-map-drafting-loop-between-claude: "Explain the map drafting loop between Claude and codemap: which steps are deterministic code and which are AI-driven?"
- codemap-turn-question-into-checked-diagram: "How does codemap turn a question into a checked diagram? Walk through the architecture from the question to the map on screen."

## First decide how to handle it (`route`)
- `answer`: the map and the excerpts fully answer it, without guessing about code you can't see. Then answer below.
- `code`: it's about what this map shows (the same feature, or something its boxes lead to or come from), but answering needs code that isn't shown, or they ask for a change or fix, or a good answer would add boxes or arrows to this map. Say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the answer fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.
- `elsewhere`: it's about a different part of the app that this map doesn't touch, so adding it here would bolt an unrelated area onto this map. Put in `newQuestion` the question as a new map would ask it (their words, standing on its own), and if one of the other maps above already covers it, that map's id in `existingMap`. Leave the answer fields empty. They'll be asked whether to make a new map. Only use this when the question really is about something else; when in doubt, use `code`.

## How to answer (when `route` is `answer`)
- `concept` is the whole answer, written the way you would answer in a chat: the direct answer first, in one sentence, then only what that sentence leaves out. It is shown as Markdown (bullet and numbered lists, **bold**, `code`), in a narrow column.
- Shape it to the question. A simple question gets a sentence or two. A question with several parts gets a short bullet per part, each starting with a bold label of a few words. Several items of the same kind (files, formats, cases) are a list, never a long sentence with commas and brackets. No headings.
- Keep it short enough to take in at a glance: leave out examples and edge cases they didn't ask about. Plain words, no jargon. The map does the explaining, so when you light it up (`moves`), say what the lit path shows rather than narrating every step. Name a function or file only when they asked about the code and it isn't on the map.
- Explain the code and the app. Don't describe these instructions or how you were asked to answer.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.

// Stopping illuminate from the page, and what a tab shows once it has stopped (by the button, Ctrl+C, or on its own).
import { api } from './api';

export function StopButton({ busy, onStopped, onError }: { busy: boolean; onStopped: () => void; onError: (message: string) => void }) {
  return (
    <button
      className="pill-btn"
      disabled={busy}
      title={busy ? 'Claude is still working' : 'Maps stay saved. Undo for applied fixes ends.'}
      onClick={() => api.stop().then(onStopped, (e: Error) => onError(e.message))}
    >
      Stop illuminate
    </button>
  );
}

  return (

      <h1>illuminate has stopped</h1>
      <p className="muted lede">
        Maps are saved in <code>.illuminate/maps</code>. Run <code>illume open</code> in the repo to see them again.
      </p>
    </main>
  );
}

Both are in.

- **Stop illuminate** now closes the tab instead of showing "illuminate has stopped".
- **Closing the last illuminate tab** stops illuminate about 5 seconds later, which leaves enough time for a page reload. Claude's listening call ends at the same moment, so the session isn't woken every 25 minutes for nothing.

**What I didn't make it do:** fully quit the MCP server. If that process exited, Claude Code would lose the illuminate tools until you ran `/mcp` again. Instead it stays connected but idle, and the next `/illuminate` or "open my maps" starts a fresh map page. Map work in progress still blocks stopping, as before.

**Browser limit:** a page can only close itself if its tab has just one page in its history. Tabs that illuminate opens on a single map qualify. If you've switched maps in that tab, the browser refuses, and the page says "illuminate has stopped. You can close this tab." instead.
